teaching_blocks.content: As-is means current, not ideal. A troublesome step still belongs if it is part of current work. Review with the people performing the process refines accuracy; it is not permission to replace current behavior with a proposed redesign.

video_need.reason: Building and reviewing a current-state BPMN map makes observed sequencing and routing concrete.

media.group_title: Represent process activities and routing with BPMN

segments.label: Build a job-application BPMN model with an interview decision
segments.summary: A hypothetical job-application process is represented in a BPMN editor. A start event connects through tasks for creating and submitting an application, attending an interview, reviewing an offer, and submitting acceptance forms, ending with the offer accepted. Sequence flows connect the activities. A gateway named “Called for interview” is then inserted after application submission. Its yes route continues to the interview, while its no route leads to an application-rejected end event. Labeling the outgoing flows makes the routing explicit.

bridge_note.before: Watch how tasks, events, sequence flows, and a gateway represent the supplied job-application scenario. Focus on the notation and routing rather than the editor-specific controls.
bridge_note.after: The clip demonstrates BPMN representation, not current-process investigation or performer validation. The text covers recording current rather than desired behavior, establishing boundaries and sequence from collected information, and reviewing accuracy with process performers.

practice_anchor.objective: Convert the hypothetical current dispatch process into an as-is BPMN diagram: begin when an order arrives, read the order, check instructions, route through requesting clarification when needed, and prepare dispatch before ending when preparation is complete. Review the diagram against supplied feedback from a process performer and correct any mismatch.
practice_anchor.success: The diagram preserves the described current activities, uses start and end events, tasks, a clarification gateway, and sequence flows, and routes both clarification outcomes to dispatch preparation. Any supplied performer correction is reflected without replacing current behavior with desired changes.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the current dispatch process visible as a BPMN diagram, showing its boundaries, ordered activities, clarification decision, conditional routes, and return to dispatch preparation.

teaching_notes: Keep improvements as a later comparison, not embedded in the as-is map.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

coverage.learning_objective: Learner can model a proposed (to-be) business process in BPMN reflecting a redesigned future state.

required_facts.statement: A future-state process map shows how the process is intended to work after improvement.
Use the current-state map to identify improvements and draw a revised map reflecting the proposed changes.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/process-mapping — Benefits of process mapping; How to create a process map

required_facts.statement: Use BPMN tasks, events, gateways, and sequence flows to represent the revised activities and routing.

teaching_blocks.content: Imagine the current dispatch map includes a separate instruction-sheet lookup and a clarification request. The team proposes a future process in which current instructions are available at the order step. A to-be map shows that intended future behavior, not a claim that the change has already happened.

teaching_blocks.title: To-Be Process Modeling
teaching_blocks.content: A future-state process map shows how the process is intended to work after improvement.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Use the current-state map to identify improvements and draw a revised map reflecting the proposed changes. Use BPMN tasks, events, gateways, and sequence flows to represent the revised activities and routing.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Use the current-state map to identify the proposed improvements. In this hypothetical redesign, replace the separate lookup with “Read current instructions on order,” and revise the routing for clarification according to the proposed behavior. Draw the changed activities using BPMN tasks, appropriate events and gateways, and sequence flows. Keep the revised map understandable as a complete proposed process rather than a few isolated change labels.

Read the old and revised sequences separately. The as-is sequence records the current lookup; the to-be sequence reflects the proposed instruction-access change. Their different meanings matter even when both use the same BPMN shapes.

The useful output is a future-state map that explicitly represents intended activities and routing after improvement. The example is a proposal, not evidence of achieved efficiency. A revised diagram can communicate how the process is meant to work while leaving implementation and actual results to their own work.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: To-be does not mean already operating. Do not describe a proposed route as observed behavior or assume that redrawing a process proves an improvement has been achieved. The model represents the intended future state.

video_need.reason: A before-and-proposed-after drawing shows how activities and routing change between maps.

practice_anchor.objective: Redesign the supplied as-is dispatch BPMN diagram to implement two stated changes: replace the separate instruction-sheet lookup with a task labeled “Read current instructions on order,” and route clarification requests only when the instructions are unclear, otherwise continuing to dispatch.
practice_anchor.success: The revised diagram represents the intended future process, includes the replacement instruction-reading task, and uses a gateway with clearly labeled routes for clarification needed and clarification not needed. Both routes connect coherently to the remaining dispatch process through BPMN sequence flows, with appropriate start and end events.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show the supplied as-is dispatch BPMN diagram beside the proposed to-be diagram, making the replacement instruction-reading task and revised clarification routing visible while distinguishing current behavior from intended future behavior.

teaching_notes: Use the current map as input; avoid claiming measured benefits from a proposal.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

coverage.learning_objective: Learner can identify gaps and bottlenecks by comparing as-is and to-be process models or examining process flow.

required_facts.statement: Process mapping can expose bottlenecks, redundant efforts, and unnecessary steps.
Inspect the mapped steps and handoffs for obstacles that impede efficient flow.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/process-mapping — How to create a process map

required_facts.statement: Compare current-state and future-state maps to identify specific differences and potential efficiency gains.
List the specific steps or handoffs where the map shows delay, redundancy, or missing work, and review these findings with process stakeholders.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/process-mapping — Benefits of process mapping; 6. Review and validate

required_facts.statement: Identify a bottleneck as a capacity-limited step that cannot keep pace, causing work to accumulate and limiting the whole workflow’s throughput, and cite the observed capacity, throughput, or accumulating-work evidence in the diagram annotation.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/bottlenecks — What is a bottleneck?; 5 strategies to rectify bottlenecks in your workflows and fix them for good — opening identification guidance

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose the dispatch map shows orders accumulating before an approval step. A delay label alone does not establish the full bottleneck explanation. In this hypothetical case, the step can handle ten orders per hour while fifteen arrive, and the waiting work grows. Annotate the map with that capacity and accumulating-work evidence: the step cannot keep pace and limits the workflow’s throughput.

teaching_blocks.title: Process Gap and Bottleneck Analysis
teaching_blocks.content: Process mapping can expose bottlenecks, redundant efforts, and unnecessary steps.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Inspect the mapped steps and handoffs for obstacles that impede efficient flow. Compare current-state and future-state maps to identify specific differences and potential efficiency gains. List the specific steps or handoffs where the map shows delay, redundancy, or missing work, and review these findings with process stakeholders. Identify a bottleneck as a capacity-limited step that cannot keep pace, causing work to accumulate and limiting the whole workflow’s throughput, and cite the observed capacity, throughput, or accumulating-work evidence in the diagram annotation.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Inspect other mapped steps and handoffs for obstacles, redundancy, or missing work. Perhaps the same instructions are copied at two handoffs. List the specific steps where the map shows those issues and review the findings with process stakeholders. Do not group every issue under “bottleneck” merely because it is inconvenient.

Compare current-state and future-state maps too. If the proposal removes one copying step, identify that concrete difference and discuss its potential efficiency gain. A map comparison identifies a proposed difference; it is not itself a measured result.

The output should connect each finding to a location in the process and supporting evidence. For the approval bottleneck, the key evidence is capacity that cannot keep pace, accumulated work, and the resulting throughput limitation. For redundant copying, the finding is repeated effort. These distinctions make the analysis more informative than marking every slow-looking box red.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Not every delay is a bottleneck. The supported bottleneck definition requires a capacity-limited step that cannot keep pace, causing accumulation and limiting throughput. Also label future-state efficiency gains as potential until supported by actual results.

video_need.reason: Showing work accumulating at a capacity-limited step and comparing mapped handoffs clarifies bottleneck evidence.

practice_anchor.objective: Annotate supplied current-state and future-state dispatch diagrams to mark the approval bottleneck and the specific difference where the proposed process removes a repeated copying step.
practice_anchor.success: The current-state approval annotation cites capacity of ten orders per hour against fifteen arriving, explains that waiting work grows and limits workflow throughput, and distinguishes this bottleneck from redundant copying. The comparison annotation identifies the removed copying step and describes reduced repeated effort as a potential efficiency gain, not a measured result.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show current-state and future-state dispatch maps side by side, with approval capacity, arrival rate, and accumulating work visible in the current state. Make the repeated copying handoffs and the proposed removal of one copying step visible, with annotations distinguishing the bottleneck from redundancy.

teaching_notes: Keep capacity examples hypothetical; distinguish bottlenecks from redundancy and missing work.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

coverage.learning_objective: Learner can apply process improvement techniques (e.g. Lean waste elimination) to redesign a process for efficiency.

required_facts.statement: Lean process improvement aims to eliminate waste and improve value delivered by a process.
Inspect a process for non-value-adding steps and propose a change that removes or reduces the identified waste.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/project-management/lean-process-improvement — How to apply Lean process improvement within projects — 1. Determine potential areas for improvement; 2. Identify potential solutions

required_facts.statement: Agree an improvement action with the team, implement it, and review its effects to continue improving the process.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/project-management/lean-process-improvement — How to apply Lean process improvement within projects

teaching_blocks.content: Imagine the process map shows dispatch instructions copied twice before preparation. The team investigates that repeated effort as a possible non-value-adding step. Lean improvement aims to eliminate waste and improve the value delivered by the process; the example is about examining a specific source of waste, not removing work simply because it takes time.

teaching_blocks.title: Process Improvement Techniques
teaching_blocks.content: Lean process improvement aims to eliminate waste and improve value delivered by a process.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Inspect a process for non-value-adding steps and propose a change that removes or reduces the identified waste. Agree an improvement action with the team, implement it, and review its effects to continue improving the process.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Inspect the copying steps and propose a change that removes or reduces the identified waste. In this hypothetical situation, the team proposes using the current instruction record instead of making a second copy. Agree the improvement action with the team, implement it, and review its effects.

The review might examine whether the repeated copying was reduced and whether the process now delivers the intended value more effectively. Those are questions for the review, not results you can infer from the proposal alone. If the effects show further issues, continue improving the process rather than treating the first change as the final answer.

The BA’s analysis connects an observed process feature, identified waste, an agreed action, and a review of effects. The technique remains grounded in the work: “remove a box from the map” is less informative than explaining which non-value-adding activity is being reduced and then checking the change.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Improvement is not synonymous with deleting as many steps as possible. Inspect for identified non-value-adding work, agree an action, and review its effects after implementation. A proposed simplification is not yet evidence that value or efficiency improved.

video_need.reason: A process example can show identified repeated effort, the proposed change, and what would be reviewed afterward.

practice_anchor.objective: For the hypothetical dispatch bottleneck caused by copying instructions twice before preparation, propose one change that reduces the identified repeated effort and justify its expected effect.
practice_anchor.success: A written proposal identifies the second copying step as the waste to reduce, describes a specific change such as using the current instruction record, and explains how it could reduce repeated effort while preserving the intended value. It distinguishes expected effects from proven results and describes agreeing the action with the team, implementing it, and reviewing whether repeated copying decreased and intended value was preserved.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show the hypothetical dispatch process with two instruction-copying steps beside a proposed process using the current instruction record instead of a second copy. Mark the repeated effort being reduced and distinguish the proposed change from effects that still need review after implementation.

teaching_notes: Do not add unsupported Lean waste categories or mandatory improvement cycles.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

coverage.learning_objective: Learner can identify and document business rules (constraints/policies) that govern process or system behavior.

required_facts.statement: Requirements documentation includes assumptions and constraints that govern the work.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/requirements-gathering — Step 4: Document requirements in one shared place

required_facts.statement: Capture required approvals and operating constraints explicitly when documenting what the deliverable must do.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/requirements-gathering — Types of project requirements to gather; Step 4

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose stakeholders say amended delivery instructions require supervisor approval. That approval governs what the deliverable must allow; it should not remain an informal comment outside the requirements record.

teaching_blocks.title: Business Rules Analysis
teaching_blocks.content: Requirements documentation includes assumptions and constraints that govern the work.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Capture required approvals and operating constraints explicitly when documenting what the deliverable must do.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
In this hypothetical entry, document “An amended instruction requires supervisor approval before dispatch preparation continues.” Record the operating constraint explicitly alongside the required behavior. If the team assumes that a supervisor is available during dispatch hours, capture that assumption too rather than leaving it hidden in the sentence.

The distinction is practical: a requested function might be displaying or amending instructions, while the governing approval or constraint limits how the work may proceed. Make those assumptions, constraints, and approvals visible in the requirement record.

Read the requirement record back to stakeholders with the approval made visible. A description that says only “Users can amend instructions” omits the stated governing condition in this example. The useful output is explicit required approval and operating-constraint information linked to what the deliverable must do. The supervisor rule is invented for the exercise, not a general policy for order services.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: An approval rule should not be left as background prose while the function is documented without it. Capture governing assumptions and constraints explicitly. Do not invent company policies or a complete business-rule classification beyond what the requirements evidence supports.

video_need.reason: The distinction and the worked business example can be understood from prose; one simple annotated visual is sufficient and a motion demonstration would mostly repeat the text.

practice_anchor.objective: Extract three business rules from this hypothetical approval process: staff can amend delivery instructions during dispatch hours only; a supervisor must approve each amendment; dispatch preparation remains paused until that approval is recorded. Write each governing condition explicitly alongside the behavior it limits.
practice_anchor.success: A written requirements record states all three conditions: amendments are limited to dispatch hours, each amendment requires supervisor approval, and dispatch preparation cannot resume until approval is recorded. Each condition is linked to the relevant required behavior, without adding unsupported policies.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show an incomplete requirement, 'Users can amend instructions,' beside an annotated requirement that makes supervisor approval and the restriction on continuing dispatch preparation explicit. Display supervisor availability during dispatch hours separately as an assumption to confirm, not an established policy.

teaching_notes: Coverage is narrow: focus on explicit approvals, assumptions, and constraints; do not expand to an unsupported rule taxonomy.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

coverage.learning_objective: Learner can build a decision table that maps combinations of condition values to the correct action/outcome.

required_facts.statement: A decision table records how combinations of conditions produce outcomes, including complex logic such as business rules.
To construct a decision table, put the conditions and resulting actions in rows and give each decision rule a column containing a unique condition combination and its associated actions.

For a limited-entry decision table, mark a condition T when satisfied, F when not satisfied, and – when irrelevant to the outcome; mark an action X when it should occur and leave it blank when it should not occur.

Check completeness by listing all condition combinations and confirming each feasible combination has a rule column with its resulting action; a feasible combination without a rule is a gap, while infeasible combinations can be removed.

Check consistency by comparing the outcomes assigned to the same feasible condition combination across the written rules and table; incompatible outcomes for that combination expose a contradiction that needs resolution.

teaching_blocks.content: Imagine a hypothetical policy with two conditions: whether an order is urgent and whether approval is present. The written rule says an urgent approved order may proceed; an urgent unapproved order requests approval; a nonurgent order may proceed regardless of approval.

teaching_blocks.title: Decision Tables
teaching_blocks.content: A decision table records how combinations of conditions produce outcomes, including complex logic such as business rules.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: To construct a decision table, put the conditions and resulting actions in rows and give each decision rule a column containing a unique condition combination and its associated actions. For a limited-entry decision table, mark a condition T when satisfied, F when not satisfied, and – when irrelevant to the outcome; mark an action X when it should occur and leave it blank when it should not occur. Check completeness by listing all condition combinations and confirming each feasible combination has a rule column with its resulting action; a feasible combination without a rule is a gap, while infeasible combinations can be removed. Check consistency by comparing the outcomes assigned to the same feasible condition combination across the written rules and table; incompatible outcomes for that combination expose a contradiction that needs resolution.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Construct a limited-entry decision table with condition rows “Urgent?” and “Approved?” and action rows “Proceed” and “Request approval.” Give each rule a column. Rule 1 has T/T and X for Proceed. Rule 2 has T/F and X for Request approval. Rule 3 has F/– and X for Proceed. Leave the other action cells blank. Here – means the approval condition is irrelevant to the nonurgent outcome, so Rule 3 covers F/T and F/F.

Check completeness by listing the feasible combinations T/T, T/F, F/T, and F/F. All four have an outcome in this example. If Rule 2 were missing, T/F would be a gap. Infeasible combinations could be removed in a different policy, but none are declared infeasible here.

Check consistency against the written rules. If another rule assigns Request approval instead of Proceed to T/T, the same feasible combination has incompatible outcomes. Record that contradiction for resolution rather than choosing one arbitrarily. The table’s job is to expose condition-to-action logic, including gaps and contradictions, not conceal uncertainty behind a neat grid.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A dash is not false: it means the condition is irrelevant to the outcome. Completeness and consistency are separate checks. A table can cover every feasible combination and still contradict the written rules by assigning incompatible outcomes to the same combination.

video_need.reason: Filling rule columns and checking every feasible combination makes dash expansion, gaps, and contradictions visible.

practice_anchor.objective: Convert the three hypothetical order rules into a decision table using manual cell entry only: urgent approved orders proceed; urgent unapproved orders request approval; nonurgent orders proceed regardless of approval. Use Urgent? and Approved? as condition rows, Proceed and Request approval as action rows, and one column per rule.
practice_anchor.success: The table represents the rules as T/T, T/F, and F/–, with X marking the appropriate action and other action cells blank. Expanding F/– confirms coverage of F/T and F/F, so all four feasible combinations have outcomes. Each outcome agrees with the written rules, with no incompatible outcomes assigned to the same combination.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the condition rows, action rows, and three rule columns visible, alongside a completeness check listing T/T, T/F, F/T, and F/F. Show that F/– covers both F/T and F/F, distinguish a missing T/F rule as a gap, and identify conflicting outcomes for T/T as a contradiction.

teaching_notes: Use conditions as rows and rules as columns; avoid reversing the brief convention.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

coverage.learning_objective: Learner can build a decision tree that represents sequential branching logic for a decision with ordered conditions.

required_facts.statement: A decision tree represents choices and possible outcomes with branches.
Start with the initial decision, add branches for the possible answers, and continue with subsequent decisions and their outcomes.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/decision-tree — How to create a decision tree

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose a hypothetical dispatch decision first asks whether an order is urgent. If yes, it next asks whether approval is present. If no, it proceeds through the nonurgent outcome. A decision tree makes that sequence of choices and possible outcomes visible with branches.

teaching_blocks.title: Decision Trees
teaching_blocks.content: A decision tree represents choices and possible outcomes with branches.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Start with the initial decision, add branches for the possible answers, and continue with subsequent decisions and their outcomes.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Start with the initial decision “Urgent?” Add one branch for yes and another for no. On the yes branch, add the subsequent decision “Approval present?” and branches for its possible answers. The approved path ends at “Proceed”; the unapproved path ends at “Request approval.” In this exercise, the no-urgency branch ends at “Proceed.” These are invented policy outcomes, not general rules for dispatch.

Read a path from the initial decision through the relevant answers to its outcome. An urgent order without approval follows yes at the first decision and no at the second, reaching Request approval. This explanation ties branch labels to decisions instead of using unlabeled lines.

The useful output is sequential branching logic. Do not add a subsequent decision to every branch merely to make the drawing symmetrical; continue where the decision being represented requires it. The tree communicates choices and outcomes, not the statistical prediction methods that may use a similarly named structure elsewhere.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A branch represents a possible answer or choice leading onward; it is not just decoration around a list of outcomes. Keep the initial and subsequent decisions visible so the reader can follow the sequence. This is business decision logic, not a machine-learning lesson.

video_need.reason: Drawing and tracing one path makes ordered decisions, answer branches, and final outcomes easy to follow.

media.group_title: From an initial choice to branching outcomes

segments.label: Build a decision tree with choices, outcome branches, and endpoints
segments.summary: A decision tree maps related choices and their possible outcomes through branches. Begin with the main decision and draw a branch for each possible action, then extend those branches to further possibilities. The example starts with choosing work or fishing. Work leads to keeping or losing a job; fishing leads to catching or not catching fish. The example assigns illustrative probabilities to these outcomes. Squares represent decisions, circles represent uncertain outcomes, and triangles mark endpoints where no further choices or uncertain outcomes remain.

bridge_note.before: Watch how the initial decision branches into actions and then outcomes. The clip uses uncertain outcomes and probabilities; focus on the branching sequence rather than treating those additions as requirements for every tree.
bridge_note.after: The clip illustrates both choices and branching construction. Devspace’s text applies these ideas to sequential yes/no business rules, using the hypothetical dispatch example rather than uncertain outcomes.

practice_anchor.objective: Arrange decision nodes, labeled answer branches, and outcome nodes on a diagram canvas to represent the hypothetical dispatch rule: check urgency first; for urgent orders, check approval; otherwise proceed.
practice_anchor.success: The diagram begins with Urgent? Its yes branch leads to Approval present?, whose yes branch ends at Proceed and whose no branch ends at Request approval. The no branch from Urgent? ends at Proceed. Each answer label is attached to the correct decision branch.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the initial Urgent? decision, its yes/no branches, the subsequent Approval present? decision on the urgent branch, and the final Proceed or Request approval outcomes visible in their correct sequence.

teaching_notes: Avoid decision-table completeness rules being silently recast as tree-specific facts.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

coverage.learning_objective: Learner can identify the entities and their attributes relevant to a business domain from a narrative description.

required_facts.statement: An entity is a business thing being described; its attributes are descriptive properties of that thing.
Identify the business things that need describing and list the descriptive attributes needed for each.

teaching_blocks.content: Imagine a stakeholder saying, “We need to describe customers and their orders, including the customer name and each order’s requested delivery date.” Start by identifying the business things being described: Customer and Order. Then separate their descriptive properties.

teaching_blocks.title: Entities and Attributes
teaching_blocks.content: An entity is a business thing being described; its attributes are descriptive properties of that thing.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Identify the business things that need describing and list the descriptive attributes needed for each.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
For this hypothetical domain, list Customer attributes such as customer name and contact number, and Order attributes such as requested delivery date and instruction text. The attribute belongs to the thing it describes. A requested delivery date describes an order in this example, while customer name describes a customer.

Read another sentence: “Dispatch staff need the instruction text for an order.” It adds a descriptive need for Order rather than automatically introducing a new entity called InstructionText. The question is which business thing needs describing and which properties are needed for that description.

The output can remain a plain list of entities with attributes. This step does not require keys, relationship symbols, or a database implementation. Those details come later. Focus first on distinguishing a business thing from a descriptive property of that thing, using the narrative as evidence rather than adding every imaginable attribute. The resulting list should answer what the business needs to describe in this example.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: An attribute is not automatically a separate entity because its name appears in a sentence. Ask whether it describes a business thing already identified. Conversely, do not merge unrelated business things into one vague entity just because they appear in the same narrative.

video_need.reason: The distinction and the worked business example can be understood from prose; one simple annotated visual is sufficient and a motion demonstration would mostly repeat the text.

practice_anchor.objective: From a supplied hypothetical narrative describing Customer and Order, identify both entities and select three explicitly supported attributes for each. The narrative must supply three descriptive properties for each business thing.
practice_anchor.success: Customer and Order are identified as entities, each has three attributes supported by the narrative, and each attribute is assigned to the business thing it describes rather than treated as a separate entity.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the distinction visible in an annotated two-column table: business thing (entity) and descriptive properties (attributes). Show Customer with customer name and contact number, and Order with requested delivery date and instruction text.

teaching_notes: Keep keys and relationships for subsequent concepts; use ordinary business descriptions first.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

coverage.learning_objective: Learner can identify the column(s) that uniquely identify each row of a table.

required_facts.statement: A primary key constraint indicates that a column, or group of columns, can be used as a unique identifier for the rows of a table; this requires the values to be both unique and not null.
A table can have at most one primary key, and a primary key can span more than one column (a composite key, composed of two or more attributes).
Entity integrity requires that every table have a primary key, and that neither the primary key nor any part of it contain null values.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose a Customer table has rows for customers 101, 102, and 103. CustomerID is a candidate for the primary key if each row’s value is unique and not null. CustomerName is less suitable in an example where two different customers share the name “North Stores”: the repeated name would not uniquely identify each row.

teaching_blocks.title: Primary Keys
teaching_blocks.content: A primary key constraint indicates that a column, or group of columns, can be used as a unique identifier for the rows of a table; this requires the values to be both unique and not null.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: A table can have at most one primary key, and a primary key can span more than one column (a composite key, composed of two or more attributes). Entity integrity requires that every table have a primary key, and that neither the primary key nor any part of it contain null values.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
A table has at most one primary key, but that key can span multiple columns. Imagine a separate table of branch-specific order numbers in which order number 7 occurs at both North and South branches. The pair BranchCode and OrderNumber can form a composite key if every pair is unique and neither part is null. One key composed of two attributes is not two primary keys.

Check the sample rows deliberately. Duplicate CustomerID values violate the uniqueness requirement. A missing CustomerID violates the not-null requirement. For a composite key, check the combination for uniqueness and every component for null values. A row with a known branch but a null order number does not meet entity integrity.

The practical result is identifying the column or column group that can uniquely identify a row while meeting the stated integrity conditions. A convenient-looking label is not enough: the actual values must satisfy uniqueness and non-null requirements.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Unique is not the whole primary-key rule: values must also be not null, and no part of a composite primary key may be null. A composite key is one primary key spanning columns, not permission to assign several primary keys to a table.

video_need.reason: Checking rows for duplicate and null single-column or composite identifiers makes the integrity requirements visible.

practice_anchor.objective: Select one valid primary key column or column group for each of three sample tables using CustomerID, CustomerName, or BranchCode and OrderNumber.
practice_anchor.success: Each selection uniquely identifies every sample row and contains no null values in any selected component. Select a single primary key per table, treating BranchCode and OrderNumber together as one composite key where neither column alone is unique.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make three sample tables visible with repeated customer names, duplicate or missing CustomerID values, and branch-specific order numbers. Highlight how uniqueness is checked for an entire column group while the not-null requirement applies to every component.

teaching_notes: Distinguish candidate examples from declared keys; avoid CREATE TABLE syntax.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

coverage.learning_objective: Learner can use a foreign key to reference another table's primary key and maintain referential integrity.

required_facts.statement: A foreign key constraint specifies that the values in a column (or group of columns) of one table must match values appearing in some row of another, referenced table.
A null foreign key value also satisfies referential integrity; a non-null one must match an existing primary key value in the referenced table.
A row whose foreign key value is not found in the referenced table is called an orphan record; referential integrity is what prevents these.

teaching_blocks.content: Imagine Customer has primary-key values 101 and 102. Order contains CustomerID to refer to a customer. An order with CustomerID 101 has a matching referenced row; a non-null CustomerID 999 does not in this hypothetical data.

teaching_blocks.title: Foreign Keys Referential Integrity
teaching_blocks.content: A foreign key constraint specifies that the values in a column (or group of columns) of one table must match values appearing in some row of another, referenced table.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: A null foreign key value also satisfies referential integrity; a non-null one must match an existing primary key value in the referenced table. A row whose foreign key value is not found in the referenced table is called an orphan record; referential integrity is what prevents these.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
The foreign-key constraint requires non-null referencing values to match a value in the referenced table. A row with 999 would be an orphan record if that value is absent from Customer. Referential integrity prevents that unmatched reference rather than making up a new customer to satisfy it.

A null foreign-key value also satisfies referential integrity under this referential-integrity rule. That is different from primary-key rules, where null is not allowed. For the exercise, distinguish three cases: matching 101, unmatched non-null 999, and null. Do not describe all three as simply “valid customer values”: null represents no known referenced value here, while 101 matches an existing customer.

A foreign key can also use a group of columns when the reference requires it. The learner’s immediate task is to check whether the referencing value or values match the required referenced row, while preserving the stated null exception. Keep the example about references and integrity rather than adding deletion or update behavior that has not been established.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: The foreign-key null rule differs from the primary-key rule. In this brief, null satisfies referential integrity; a non-null value must match. Do not treat an unmatched non-null value as an acceptable unknown.

video_need.reason: Tracing matching, null, and orphan references across two small tables clarifies referential integrity.

practice_anchor.objective: Using Customer with primary-key CustomerID values 101 and 102 and Order with CustomerID values 101, 999, and null, select the foreign-key field and identify the referencing value that violates referential integrity.
practice_anchor.success: Identifies Order.CustomerID as the foreign key referencing Customer.CustomerID, flags 999 as an unmatched non-null reference creating an orphan record, and distinguishes matching 101 and permitted null from the violation.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show Customer and Order side by side, with Customer.CustomerID marked as the primary key and Order.CustomerID as the foreign key. Make the matching reference 101, unmatched reference 999, and null reference visible and distinguish their referential-integrity status.

teaching_notes: Do not invent cascade behavior or NULL prohibitions beyond the brief.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

coverage.learning_objective: Learner can recognize and model a one-to-many relationship between two entities.

required_facts.statement: In a one-to-many (1:M) relationship, one row on the 'one' side relates to many rows on the 'many' side; for example, one department has many employees.

In the Customer/Order example, a customer can place a minimum of zero and a maximum of many orders, while an order relates to a maximum of one customer, so Order is the 'many' side (the many side is optional, since a customer doesn't need to place an order to be a customer); the foreign key CustID is placed in the Order table and must match a valid CustID in the Customer table.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose Customer has one row for customer 101 and one for customer 102. Order has three rows referencing 101 and no rows referencing 102. One customer can therefore relate to many orders, while the example allows a customer to have zero orders.

teaching_blocks.title: One To Many
teaching_blocks.content: In a one-to-many (1:M) relationship, one row on the 'one' side relates to many rows on the 'many' side; for example, one department has many employees.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: In the Customer/Order example, a customer can place a minimum of zero and a maximum of many orders, while an order relates to a maximum of one customer, so Order is the 'many' side (the many side is optional, since a customer doesn't need to place an order to be a customer); the foreign key CustID is placed in the Order table and must match a valid CustID in the Customer table.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Identify Order as the many side. Its CustID foreign key stores the reference to a valid Customer CustID. The same customer identifier can appear on multiple order rows because those rows are different orders belonging to the same customer. The Customer side has the customer row being referenced.

Read the allowed counts in both directions. Customer 101 has several orders; customer 102 has none and still exists as a customer. Each order relates to a maximum of one customer in the stated example. Do not reverse the relationship merely because the customer name is shown on an order report.

The useful modeling decision is not just naming “one-to-many.” It is identifying which thing can have many related instances and placing the reference on that many side. The zero-order customer also shows why “many” should not be interpreted as requiring at least one order in this example. These counts are the business rules of the Customer/Order example, not universal counts for every relationship.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: One-to-many does not mean every one-side row already has several related rows. The stated customer example permits zero orders. Nor should the foreign key be placed on Customer just because that is the one side: CustID belongs in Order for this relationship.

video_need.reason: Linking one customer to several orders and another to none makes direction, optionality, and foreign-key placement visible.

practice_anchor.objective: Model the stated Customer/Order relationship by selecting the one and many sides, assigning the allowed counts in each direction, and selecting the table that holds the CustID foreign key and the field it references.
practice_anchor.success: Customer is identified as the one side and Order as the many side. A customer may have zero to many orders, and an order relates to a maximum of one customer. Order.CustID references Customer.CustID, and every supplied Order.CustID matches an existing Customer.CustID.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show Customer rows for CustID 101 and 102 alongside three distinct Order rows referencing CustID 101 and none referencing 102. Highlight Order.CustID as the foreign key referencing Customer.CustID, making repeated references and the valid zero-order customer visible.

teaching_notes: Preserve the zero-to-many customer example and maximum-one wording for an order.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

coverage.learning_objective: Learner can recognize a many-to-many relationship and resolve it with a junction/bridge table.

required_facts.statement: A many-to-many (M:N) relationship cannot be implemented directly in the relational model; it is resolved into two one-to-many relationships using a composite entity, also called a junction or bridge table.
The junction table must contain at least the primary keys of the two original tables, used as foreign keys, and may also contain additional attributes of its own.
The combination of the two original tables' primary keys, brought in as foreign keys, will make the primary key of the junction table (or, together with another attribute, can form it).
source_refs: database_design_open_textbook#ch8-Example of mapping an M:N binary relationship type

teaching_blocks.content: Imagine orders can include several products, and a product can appear in several orders. That is a many-to-many relationship. In the relational model described here, resolve it using a junction table rather than attempting to implement the many-to-many relationship directly.

teaching_blocks.title: Many To Many Junction Tables
teaching_blocks.content: A many-to-many (M:N) relationship cannot be implemented directly in the relational model; it is resolved into two one-to-many relationships using a composite entity, also called a junction or bridge table.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: The junction table must contain at least the primary keys of the two original tables, used as foreign keys, and may also contain additional attributes of its own. The combination of the two original tables' primary keys, brought in as foreign keys, will make the primary key of the junction table (or, together with another attribute, can form it).

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
For this hypothetical model, create OrderProduct between Order and Product. It contains OrderID and ProductID, brought in from the original primary keys and used as foreign keys. It may also contain its own attribute, such as quantity. The two original tables now each have a one-to-many relationship with OrderProduct.

Example junction rows are (Order 10, Product A, quantity 2), (Order 10, Product B, quantity 1), and (Order 11, Product A, quantity 3). Order 10 links to two products, and Product A links to two orders. The pair of original identifiers forms the junction primary key in this example. Where needed, those identifiers together with another attribute can form the key.

The important change is the representation of each association as a junction row. Quantity describes that association here, not every occurrence of Product A in every order. Keep both original references visible so the model does not lose one side of the relationship when resolving it.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A junction table is not simply a copy of one original table. It contains at least both original primary keys as foreign keys, and its key uses their combination or that combination with another attribute. Resolving M:N produces two 1:M relationships.

video_need.reason: Transforming a many-to-many association into junction rows and two one-to-many links makes the resolution understandable.

practice_anchor.objective: Design OrderProduct for the hypothetical Order–Product scenario by selecting its fields, marking both foreign keys, and selecting the fields that form its primary key. Include quantity as an attribute of each order–product association.
practice_anchor.success: OrderProduct contains OrderID and ProductID as foreign keys referencing the original tables, quantity as an association attribute, and the pair OrderID–ProductID as its primary key. Each original table has a one-to-many relationship with OrderProduct.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show OrderProduct with OrderID and ProductID marked as foreign keys and jointly as its primary key, alongside quantity. Include rows (10, A, 2), (10, B, 1), and (11, A, 3), making visible that one order can reference several products and one product can appear in several orders.

teaching_notes: Do not introduce alternative surrogate-key designs beyond this brief.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

coverage.learning_objective: Learner can determine and notate the cardinality (one-to-many, many-to-many) of a relationship between two entities using crow's-foot notation.

required_facts.statement: Relationship cardinality expresses how many instances on either side can be related.
A one-to-many relationship has a column with unique values on one side and potentially repeated matching values on the other.
A many-to-many relationship permits repeated matching values on both sides.
Determine the relationship by checking whether each side permits one or multiple matching instances.
In crow’s-foot notation, a circle (ring) represents zero, a bar (dash) represents one, and a crow’s-foot represents many.
Pair a circle and bar for optional zero-or-one, two bars for mandatory exactly-one, a circle and crow’s-foot for optional zero-or-many, or a bar and crow’s-foot for mandatory one-or-many.
At each relationship end, place the minimum symbol inward and the maximum symbol closest to the entity box.
Draw a relationship line between the entities and annotate both ends with the symbol pair for the number of instances of that end’s entity that can relate to an instance of the other entity.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose business rules say a customer may have zero or many orders, while each order must relate to exactly one customer. Cardinality expresses permitted counts, not merely the number of rows currently in a sample.

teaching_blocks.title: Relationships and Cardinality
teaching_blocks.content: Relationship cardinality expresses how many instances on either side can be related.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: A one-to-many relationship has a column with unique values on one side and potentially repeated matching values on the other. A many-to-many relationship permits repeated matching values on both sides. Determine the relationship by checking whether each side permits one or multiple matching instances. In crow’s-foot notation, a circle (ring) represents zero, a bar (dash) represents one, and a crow’s-foot represents many. Pair a circle and bar for optional zero-or-one, two bars for mandatory exactly-one, a circle and crow’s-foot for optional zero-or-many, or a bar and crow’s-foot for mandatory one-or-many. At each relationship end, place the minimum symbol inward and the maximum symbol closest to the entity box. Draw a relationship line between the entities and annotate both ends with the symbol pair for the number of instances of that end’s entity that can relate to an instance of the other entity.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Check each direction: one customer can match multiple orders, and one order matches one customer. In crow’s-foot notation, place circle plus crow’s-foot at the Order end for zero-or-many orders per customer. Place two bars at the Customer end for mandatory exactly-one customer per order. At each end, put the minimum symbol inward and the maximum symbol closest to the entity box.

The symbols carry separate meanings: circle means zero, bar means one, and crow’s-foot means many. Circle plus bar would mean optional zero-or-one; bar plus crow’s-foot would mean mandatory one-or-many. Use the pair appropriate to the actual business rule instead of choosing whichever shape fits the available space.

The data perspective also helps: one-to-many has unique values on one side and potentially repeated matching values on the other; many-to-many permits repeated matching values on both sides. Determine the relationship by checking whether each side permits one or multiple matching instances. The example’s mandatory order-to-customer rule is a hypothetical business rule for this diagram, not inferred solely from observing one current order.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A relationship end describes how many instances of that end’s entity can relate to an instance of the opposite entity. Reading the crow’s-foot as the count of customers instead of orders reverses the example. A current sample also does not by itself establish all permitted counts.

video_need.reason: Annotating both relationship ends makes crow’s-foot direction, minimum, and maximum counts visible.

media.group_title: Read relationship counts and annotate both ends

segments.label: Determine minimum and maximum counts at each relationship end
segments.summary: Cardinality describes how many instances of one entity can relate to an instance of another. A circle represents zero, a bar represents one, and a crow’s-foot represents many. Determine the minimum and maximum separately in each direction. In the customer–order example, each order relates to exactly one customer, while a customer may have zero or many orders. In the order–order item example, each item relates to exactly one order, while each order has one or many items. These counts express the business rules assumed in the examples.

segments.label: Recognize one-to-many and many-to-many from matching values
segments.summary: Comparing matching CustomerID values illustrates relationship types. Two customer tables with unique CustomerID values on both sides illustrate one-to-one. Customers with unique CustomerID values matched to orders with repeated CustomerID values illustrate one-to-many; an individual customer having only one order does not change that classification. Reversing the sides gives many-to-one. In the final example, CustomerID repeats in both customer-segment records and orders, illustrating many-to-many: multiple orders can match multiple segment records for the same customer. These examples illustrate matching patterns; permitted counts must still follow the business rules.

bridge_note.before: Watch the first clip for counts in each direction; its “vertical line” is Devspace’s bar. The second compares matching values. Treat example policies as hypothetical and sample rows as illustrations, not proof of every permitted count.
bridge_note.after: The first clip does not explain unique-versus-repeated matching columns; the second does not teach crow’s-foot notation. The text covers both perspectives, the standalone definition and directional method, all four symbol pairs, minimum/maximum placement, and how to draw and annotate both ends.

practice_anchor.objective: Use entity boxes, relationship lines, and a crow’s-foot symbol palette to determine and draw cardinality for two supplied hypothetical entity pairs: Customer–Order and Customer–Segment. Apply these rules: a customer may have zero or many orders, and each order must have exactly one customer; a customer may belong to zero or many segments, and each segment must contain one or many customers.
practice_anchor.success: Customer–Order is identified as one-to-many, with two bars at Customer and circle plus crow’s-foot at Order. Customer–Segment is identified as many-to-many, with bar plus crow’s-foot at Customer and circle plus crow’s-foot at Segment. Both relationships have a connecting line, annotations at both ends, minimum symbols inward, and maximum symbols closest to the entity boxes.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make both annotated relationship ends visible for Customer–Order and Customer–Segment, with entity boxes, connecting lines, and clearly distinguishable minimum and maximum symbols. Show which opposite-entity instance each end’s counts refer to.

teaching_notes: Keep minimum/maximum symbol ordering explicit and do not confuse cardinality with observed row counts.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

coverage.learning_objective: Learner can draw an entity-relationship diagram representing entities, attributes, and relationships for a business domain.

required_facts.statement: A model diagram can show entity types, their attributes, and relationships between instances.

Draw named entity boxes with relevant attributes, clearly identify primary-key and foreign-key attributes, and connect related entities through each foreign key and its referenced key, marking the permitted multiplicities.
Use multiplicity labels such as 1, 0..1, 0..*, or 1..* to state the permitted numbers of related instances.

teaching_blocks.content: Imagine a business model containing Customer and Order. Draw a named box for each entity and list relevant attributes. For this hypothetical diagram, Customer contains CustomerID and Name; Order contains OrderID, CustomerID, and RequestedDate. Clearly identify CustomerID as Customer’s primary key, OrderID as Order’s primary key, and Order.CustomerID as a foreign key.

teaching_blocks.title: Entity-Relationship Diagrams
teaching_blocks.content: A model diagram can show entity types, their attributes, and relationships between instances.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Draw named entity boxes with relevant attributes, clearly identify primary-key and foreign-key attributes, and connect related entities through each foreign key and its referenced key, marking the permitted multiplicities. Use multiplicity labels such as 1, 0..1, 0..*, or 1..* to state the permitted numbers of related instances.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Connect the foreign-key attribute to its referenced key. Mark permitted multiplicities on the relationship: suppose every order belongs to exactly one customer and each customer may have zero or many orders. Use 1 at the Customer end and 0..* at the Order end for those rules. A 0..1 label would instead allow zero or one; 1..* would require one or many.

Read the diagram back in business language. It says which things are described, what properties they have, how their instances relate, and how many related instances are permitted. The links should correspond to the identified keys rather than being arbitrary lines between boxes.

The result is an entity-relationship diagram, not just a list of tables. The particular attributes and mandatory customer rule are invented for this exercise. In actual modeling, use the established domain information and permitted counts rather than borrowing this example’s rules automatically.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Two boxes joined by an unlabeled line do not communicate the full permitted multiplicities. Likewise, identifying keys without connecting a foreign key to its referenced key leaves the intended relationship unclear. Keep both structural links and allowed counts visible.

video_need.reason: Drawing boxes, identifying keys, and labeling relationship ends shows how the diagram communicates a model.

practice_anchor.objective: Draw and submit an ERD for the hypothetical Customer and Order scenario. Include CustomerID and Name in Customer, and OrderID, CustomerID, and RequestedDate in Order. Represent the rules that each order belongs to exactly one customer and each customer may have zero or many orders.
practice_anchor.success: The submitted diagram contains named Customer and Order boxes with the specified attributes; identifies Customer.CustomerID and Order.OrderID as primary keys and Order.CustomerID as a foreign key; connects Order.CustomerID to Customer.CustomerID; and labels the Customer end 1 and the Order end 0..*.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the Customer and Order entity boxes, their attributes, primary-key and foreign-key markings, the connection between Order.CustomerID and Customer.CustomerID, and the permitted multiplicities at both relationship ends visible.

teaching_notes: Avoid tool-specific ERD commands or additional notation not in the facts.
