teaching_blocks.title: Current-State Capability Assessment
teaching_blocks.content: A current-state assessment describes the present situation as a baseline for identifying improvements.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Record detailed notes about the current business situation in a structured current-state column. Organize the current-state notes by the business areas being assessed so they can be compared with goals and gaps.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Put detailed current-state notes in a structured current-state column. Organize them by business area: instruction access, handoffs, and dispatch preparation. That organization makes later comparison possible without mixing every observation into one vague statement such as “the process is inefficient.”

For instruction access, the example note might be “Staff consult a separate sheet for current instructions.” For handoffs, it might describe who supplies amended information. If the scenario provides a measured preparation time, record it with its context. Do not invent a baseline number merely because a later target will need comparison.

The output is a description of the present business situation arranged by the areas being assessed. It is not yet a list of desired changes. Keep an observed condition, a proposed improvement, and a judgment about success separate. This way a reader can see what current situation the subsequent goals and gaps refer to, rather than having to reconstruct the baseline from the recommendation.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Current-state assessment is not a wish list. A note saying “use one instruction record” describes a desired change, not the current situation. Record the baseline in the current-state column and organize it by the assessed business areas.

video_need.reason: The distinction and the worked business example can be understood from prose; one simple annotated visual is sufficient and a motion demonstration would mostly repeat the text.

practice_anchor.objective: Write a current-state capability assessment for the supplied hypothetical dispatch situation in a table with Business area and Current state columns. Organize detailed baseline notes under instruction access, handoffs, and dispatch preparation.
practice_anchor.success: Each business area has current-state notes grounded in the supplied situation. The notes describe present conditions rather than desired changes, retain any supplied measurement context without inventing numbers, and provide an organized baseline for later comparison with goals and gaps.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make visible a two-column assessment organized by instruction access, handoffs, and dispatch preparation. Annotate the Current state column to show detailed present-condition notes, distinguish them from desired changes, and explain how grouping notes by business area supports later comparison.

teaching_notes: Stay with structured baseline notes; do not assume measurements absent from the situation.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

coverage.learning_objective: Learner can define a future-state vision describing the desired target state an initiative should achieve.

required_facts.statement: A desired-state definition states the objectives and situation the business wants to achieve.
Express the goal using a business outcome and measurable success target.
Write the desired objectives alongside the corresponding business areas in the desired-state column.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose the current-state assessment records lengthy dispatch preparation and unclear instruction access. Future-state vision states the objectives and situation the business wants to achieve, with a business outcome and measurable success target.

teaching_blocks.title: Future-State Vision Definition
teaching_blocks.content: A desired-state definition states the objectives and situation the business wants to achieve.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Express the goal using a business outcome and measurable success target. Write the desired objectives alongside the corresponding business areas in the desired-state column.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
For this hypothetical effort, a desired objective could be “Dispatch staff prepare orders with current instructions, with preparation completed within five minutes in the stated operating conditions.” The five-minute target is an example business decision, not a standard for every dispatch operation. It gives the desired state more substance than “make dispatch better.”

Write desired objectives in the desired-state column beside the corresponding business areas. The instruction-access objective belongs alongside the instruction-access baseline; the preparation target belongs alongside the preparation baseline. Keeping that alignment visible lets readers compare like areas rather than comparing a broad aspiration with an unrelated current note.

The useful output is a future situation described in terms of business outcome and success target. It does not need to name a particular tool as the vision. “Purchase software” states an action, while “staff have current instructions and meet the preparation target” describes what the business wants to achieve. Keep the target’s conditions visible so its meaning is not lost in a slogan.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A future-state vision is not merely a named solution or a favorable adjective. State the desired business outcome with a measurable success target. It is intended future behavior, not evidence that the business has already reached that state.

video_need.reason: The distinction and the worked business example can be understood from prose; one simple annotated visual is sufficient and a motion demonstration would mostly repeat the text.

practice_anchor.objective: For the hypothetical dispatch effort, write a future-state vision describing staff preparing orders with current instructions and completing preparation within five minutes under the stated operating conditions. Enter the desired objectives in the desired-state column beside the corresponding instruction-access and preparation business areas; no formulas are needed.
practice_anchor.success: The statement describes the intended business situation rather than a tool purchase, includes the five-minute preparation target with its operating conditions, and places each desired objective beside its corresponding business area. The target is treated as a decision for this hypothetical effort, not a universal standard.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show instruction access and dispatch preparation as separate business-area rows, with current-state notes and aligned desired-state objectives. Annotate the desired objectives to distinguish the business outcome from the measurable preparation target and its stated operating conditions.

teaching_notes: Do not turn the desired target into an unsupported universal service level.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

coverage.learning_objective: Learner can identify the gap between current state and future state and articulate what must change to close it.

required_facts.statement: A gap is a specific difference between the current situation and the desired state.
Compare the current-state description with the desired-state objectives and list the specific differences keeping the business from those goals.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/software/confluence/templates/gap-analysis — Assess current state; Define the desired state; Identify gaps

teaching_blocks.content: Imagine the current-state column says dispatch preparation takes twelve minutes under the assessed conditions, while the desired-state column sets a five-minute target under the same conditions. The specific time difference is seven minutes. Another current note says staff consult two instruction sources, while the desired state calls for current instructions available in one place.

teaching_blocks.title: Gap Identification and Analysis
teaching_blocks.content: A gap is a specific difference between the current situation and the desired state.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Compare the current-state description with the desired-state objectives and list the specific differences keeping the business from those goals.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Compare each current description with its corresponding desired objective. List the specific differences keeping the business from the goal: the preparation-time difference and the information-access difference in this hypothetical case. These are more precise than writing only “there is a dispatch gap.”

Keep the comparison tied to the descriptions supplied. If the current-state record contains no preparation-time measurement, do not calculate a numerical difference by inventing one. You can still identify the documented qualitative difference and preserve any missing information as a question.

The output is a gap list grounded in current and desired states. It does not itself prove the cause of every gap or choose the solution. The immediate analytical task is to make the difference explicit enough that stakeholders can see what has to change. The example’s numbers and one-place objective illustrate that comparison, not a claim about a real organization.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A gap is the difference between current and desired states, not simply a complaint or a proposed fix. “Buy a new system” does not identify the difference. Compare corresponding descriptions and state what separates the business from its goal.

video_need.reason: The distinction and the worked business example can be understood from prose; one simple annotated visual is sufficient and a motion demonstration would mostly repeat the text.

practice_anchor.objective: Compare the supplied current- and desired-state descriptions for dispatch preparation and select the concrete differences to include in a gap list.
practice_anchor.success: The gap list identifies the seven-minute preparation-time difference and the difference between consulting two instruction sources and having current instructions available in one place, without substituting a complaint, inferred cause, or proposed fix.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show aligned current-state, desired-state, and specific-gap columns for the hypothetical dispatch example: twelve versus five minutes gives a seven-minute difference; two instruction sources versus current instructions in one place gives an information-access difference.

teaching_notes: Do not infer root causes or guaranteed solutions from a gap alone.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

coverage.learning_objective: Learner can conduct a SWOT analysis identifying strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats for a business situation.

required_facts.statement: SWOT separates strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats in a business situation.
Strengths are internal advantages; weaknesses are internal limitations.
Opportunities are favorable external possibilities; threats are external factors that could harm success.
Create four labeled quadrants and place each factor according to whether it is internal or external and favorable or unfavorable.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/strategic-planning/swot-analysis — How to conduct a SWOT analysis

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose an order-service team is assessing a business situation. Its experienced dispatch staff are an internal advantage, while fragmented instruction records are an internal limitation. A new external delivery partnership may create a favorable possibility, while an external competitor’s improved service may threaten success.

teaching_blocks.title: SWOT Analysis
teaching_blocks.content: SWOT separates strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats in a business situation.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Strengths are internal advantages; weaknesses are internal limitations. Opportunities are favorable external possibilities; threats are external factors that could harm success. Create four labeled quadrants and place each factor according to whether it is internal or external and favorable or unfavorable.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Create four labeled quadrants: Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, and Threats. Place experienced staff under Strengths and fragmented records under Weaknesses. Place the partnership possibility under Opportunities and the competitor factor under Threats. These are hypothetical factors selected to make the two distinctions clear.

For each placement, ask two questions: is the factor internal or external, and favorable or unfavorable? Strong staff and the partnership are both favorable, but one is internal and the other external. Fragmentation and the competitor factor are both unfavorable, but they also belong on different sides of that distinction.

The useful result is an organized view of the situation rather than an unclassified list of positive and negative comments. Do not classify solely by whether a factor sounds important. A favorable external possibility belongs under Opportunities even if the team hopes to benefit from it internally. Keep the classification tied to the factor being described.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Strengths and opportunities are not interchangeable synonyms for positives; internal versus external distinguishes them. The same distinction separates weaknesses from threats. A four-quadrant layout helps only when each factor is placed using both dimensions.

video_need.reason: A simple labeled four-quadrant visual is enough; motion would mostly repeat the classifications.

practice_anchor.objective: Build a four-quadrant SWOT matrix for the hypothetical order-service team by placing experienced dispatch staff, fragmented instruction records, a possible external delivery partnership, and an external competitor’s improved service into the labeled quadrants.
practice_anchor.success: The matrix has Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, and Threats quadrants. Experienced dispatch staff are placed under Strengths, fragmented instruction records under Weaknesses, the possible external delivery partnership under Opportunities, and the competitor’s improved service under Threats, using both internal versus external and favorable versus unfavorable distinctions.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show a four-quadrant SWOT matrix with Strengths and Weaknesses identified as internal, Opportunities and Threats as external, and the favorable versus unfavorable distinction visible. Place each of the four order-service factors in its corresponding quadrant.

teaching_notes: Avoid scoring SWOT factors or implying SWOT proves causation.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

coverage.learning_objective: Learner can prioritize requirements using MoSCoW categories: Must, Should, Could, Won't have.

required_facts.statement: MoSCoW groups requirements as Must have, Should have, Could have, or Will not have for the scope being prioritized.
Must-have items are essential: without them the solution would not work or the project would be useless.
Should-have items are important but the solution can still work without them.
Could-have items are desirable but nonessential and have a smaller impact if omitted.
Will-not-have items are not needed within the prioritization scope and can be deprioritized or dropped.
Define the prioritization scope, discuss each item’s importance, and assign the category the group agrees fits it.

teaching_blocks.content: Imagine prioritizing requirements for an initial delivery-instruction release. Define that scope before assigning MoSCoW categories. In this hypothetical scope, seeing current instructions is essential: without it, the solution would not work for its stated purpose, so the group assigns Must have.

teaching_blocks.title: MoSCoW Prioritization
teaching_blocks.content: MoSCoW groups requirements as Must have, Should have, Could have, or Will not have for the scope being prioritized.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Must-have items are essential: without them the solution would not work or the project would be useless. Should-have items are important but the solution can still work without them. Could-have items are desirable but nonessential and have a smaller impact if omitted. Will-not-have items are not needed within the prioritization scope and can be deprioritized or dropped. Define the prioritization scope, discuss each item’s importance, and assign the category the group agrees fits it.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
An amendment indicator is important but the solution can still work without it, so it is a Should have in this example. A convenience color choice is desirable, nonessential, and has a smaller omission impact, so it is a Could have. A vehicle-purchasing feature is not needed within this scope, so it is Will not have. The same labels are not universal classifications of those features; they depend on the agreed scope and importance.

Discuss each item’s importance and assign the category the group agrees fits. Keep the reasoning attached to the category so Must have is not simply a synonym for “a stakeholder wants it strongly.” Should have and Could have both allow a working solution without the item, but the described importance and omission impact differ.

The practical output is scope-specific grouping that distinguishes essential work from important, desirable, or excluded work. Will not have refers to what is not needed within the prioritization scope; it need not be rewritten as a claim that the organization must never consider that item.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: MoSCoW categories are not just four levels of enthusiasm. Must have is essential to a working or useful solution in the stated scope. Will not have is scope-specific, not necessarily a permanent ban. Define the scope and discuss importance before assigning labels.

video_need.reason: The distinction and the worked business example can be understood from prose; one simple annotated visual is sufficient and a motion demonstration would mostly repeat the text.

practice_anchor.objective: Categorize eight given requirements for the hypothetical initial delivery-instruction release as Must have, Should have, Could have, or Will not have. Use the stated scope and each requirement's importance and omission impact to justify each assignment.
practice_anchor.success: All eight requirements receive categories consistent with the stated scope and supplied importance information. Justifications distinguish essential requirements from important but nonessential requirements, lower-impact desirable requirements, and requirements not needed within scope.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the agreed initial delivery-instruction release scope visible above an annotated table linking current instructions, an amendment indicator, a convenience color choice, and a vehicle-purchasing feature to their respective MoSCoW categories and scope-specific reasons.

teaching_notes: Keep “Will not have” terminology from the brief; no unsupported percentage allocations.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

coverage.learning_objective: Learner can classify features using the Kano model (basic, performance, delighter) to understand their effect on satisfaction.

required_facts.statement: Kano classifies features by how functionality relates to customer satisfaction.
Must-be or basic features are expected; their absence causes dissatisfaction, while their presence adds little satisfaction.
Performance features produce more satisfaction as their functionality improves.
Attractive or excitement features can delight users who did not expect them and may not notice their absence.
Use user evidence about satisfaction and the feature’s functionality to classify and discuss the appropriate category.
Indifferent features are those users feel neutral toward: changes in their functionality do not significantly increase or decrease customer satisfaction.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose user evidence about an order service shows several different satisfaction patterns. Users expect their current instructions to be accurate and are dissatisfied when they are missing; providing them adds little extra satisfaction. That pattern fits a Must-be or basic feature.

teaching_blocks.title: Kano Analysis
teaching_blocks.content: Kano classifies features by how functionality relates to customer satisfaction.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Must-be or basic features are expected; their absence causes dissatisfaction, while their presence adds little satisfaction. Performance features produce more satisfaction as their functionality improves. Attractive or excitement features can delight users who did not expect them and may not notice their absence. Use user evidence about satisfaction and the feature’s functionality to classify and discuss the appropriate category. Indifferent features are those users feel neutral toward: changes in their functionality do not significantly increase or decrease customer satisfaction.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Evidence might show that progressively quicker instruction access produces more satisfaction: that is a Performance pattern. An unexpected helpful suggestion could delight users while its absence goes unnoticed: that is an Attractive or excitement pattern. If users remain neutral as a feature’s functionality changes, it is Indifferent.

Classify using evidence about satisfaction and functionality, not the BA’s personal excitement about an idea. In this hypothetical case, the same design team might find a decorative feature exciting while user evidence shows neutrality. The evidence would support Indifferent rather than Attractive.

The useful output is a discussion of how functionality relates to satisfaction. These categories do not state delivery priority by themselves. A feature being expected is a satisfaction pattern, while a separate prioritization decision asks what belongs in the delivery scope.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Attractive means it can delight users who did not expect it; it does not mean the team likes the feature. Basic features can cause dissatisfaction when absent even though their presence adds little satisfaction. Preserve that asymmetry instead of treating all features as linear satisfaction gains.

video_need.reason: Contrasting expected, improving, surprising, and neutral satisfaction patterns benefits from visual curves or changing states.

practice_anchor.objective: Classify five given features of the hypothetical order service as Must-be/basic, Performance, Attractive/excitement, or Indifferent, using supplied user evidence about functionality and satisfaction. Provide a justification for each classification.
practice_anchor.success: All five features are matched to the category supported by the supplied evidence. Each justification explains the relevant satisfaction pattern: dissatisfaction when an expected feature is absent, increasing satisfaction as functionality improves, unexpected delight with little response to absence, or neutrality as functionality changes.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the four Kano satisfaction patterns visible side by side, contrasting user responses when functionality is absent, present, or improved. Label Must-be/basic, Performance, Attractive/excitement, and Indifferent, and connect each pattern to user evidence from the hypothetical order service.

teaching_notes: Include Indifferent; avoid adding unsupported Kano categories or survey procedures.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

coverage.learning_objective: Learner can build a weighted scoring model that ranks requirements/options by weighted criteria totals.

required_facts.statement: A weighted decision matrix compares options on criteria whose weights represent importance.
List the criteria and options, assign criterion weights, and score every option against each criterion using a consistent scale.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/software/confluence/templates/decision-matrix — Define decision criteria; Assign weights; List the options; Score each option

required_facts.statement: Multiply each criterion score by its weight and add those products for the option’s total weighted score.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/software/confluence/templates/decision-matrix — Calculate the weighted scores and make a decision

required_facts.statement: Compare the totals to rank the options; the highest total is typically the best choice under the chosen criteria and weights.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/software/confluence/templates/decision-matrix — Calculate the weighted scores and make a decision

teaching_blocks.content: Imagine comparing two hypothetical instruction-access options on clarity and implementation fit. Assign importance weights 0.6 to clarity and 0.4 to fit. Use a consistent scale where higher scores are better. Option A scores 4 and 2; Option B scores 3 and 4.

teaching_blocks.title: Weighted Scoring Models
teaching_blocks.content: A weighted decision matrix compares options on criteria whose weights represent importance.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: List the criteria and options, assign criterion weights, and score every option against each criterion using a consistent scale. Multiply each criterion score by its weight and add those products for the option’s total weighted score. Compare the totals to rank the options; the highest total is typically the best choice under the chosen criteria and weights.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Multiply each score by its criterion weight and add the products. A totals 4 × 0.6 + 2 × 0.4 = 3.2. B totals 3 × 0.6 + 4 × 0.4 = 3.4. B ranks higher under these chosen criteria, weights, and scores.

The highest total is typically the best choice under the chosen setup, not a universal fact that B is best in every context. The weights represent importance, and the scores express performance on the consistent scale. Record them so another reader can understand the comparison rather than seeing only the final total.

The practical output is an explicit weighted comparison of options. If a stakeholder challenges the recommendation, return to the criteria, importance weights, and scores. Do not defend 3.4 as if it were independent of those choices. The example weights sum to one; the key calculation is score times weight, summed across criteria.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Adding unweighted scores is not the weighted-total calculation. Multiply each criterion score by its importance weight first. Also keep the qualification: the highest total is typically best under the chosen criteria and weights, not proof of an objectively best solution in all circumstances.

video_need.reason: A worked matrix can show score-by-weight products and how they combine into option totals.

practice_anchor.objective: Use a supplied decision matrix to score four hypothetical instruction-access options against three criteria with given importance weights. Apply the same supplied higher-is-better scale to every option, multiply each score by its criterion weight, add the products, and rank the options.
practice_anchor.success: Every option has a score for each criterion on the supplied scale, each weighted product and total is calculated correctly, and the four options are ranked from highest to lowest total. The highest-ranked option is identified as typically best under the chosen criteria, weights, and scores.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make visible a decision matrix containing four instruction-access options, three criteria, their importance weights, consistent-scale scores, score-by-weight products, option totals, and the resulting ranking.

teaching_notes: Preserve “typically”; do not prescribe weight normalization as mandatory.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

coverage.learning_objective: Learner can evaluate multiple candidate solutions/vendors against defined criteria and recommend the best fit.

required_facts.statement: Solution comparison uses defined decision criteria rather than an unstructured preference.
Score each candidate solution against the same criteria and multiply the scores by the corresponding importance weights.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/software/confluence/templates/decision-matrix — Score each option; Calculate the weighted scores

required_facts.statement: Sum each candidate’s weighted scores, compare the totals, and explain the recommendation in terms of the criteria and scores.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/software/confluence/templates/decision-matrix — Calculate the weighted scores and make a decision

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose stakeholders are choosing between two instruction-access solutions. Define shared criteria before comparing them: instruction clarity and fit with the agreed operating constraints. For this hypothetical assessment, use weights 0.6 and 0.4 and a common score scale.

teaching_blocks.title: Solution Option Evaluation and Recommendation
teaching_blocks.content: Solution comparison uses defined decision criteria rather than an unstructured preference.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Score each candidate solution against the same criteria and multiply the scores by the corresponding importance weights. Sum each candidate’s weighted scores, compare the totals, and explain the recommendation in terms of the criteria and scores.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Solution A scores 4 for clarity and 2 for fit, giving 4 × 0.6 + 2 × 0.4 = 3.2. Solution B scores 3 and 4, giving 3 × 0.6 + 4 × 0.4 = 3.4. Compare the totals and recommend B on this assessment, explaining that its stronger fit outweighs A’s clarity advantage under the selected weights.

The recommendation should point back to the criteria and scores. “We prefer B” omits the analytical basis; “B totals 3.4 under the agreed clarity and fit assessment” makes that basis visible. The two totals are hypothetical and depend on the chosen assessment, not a claim about real products.

The useful BA output is a reasoned solution recommendation, not only a completed matrix. State what was compared, how importance affected the scores, and how the resulting totals support the recommendation. Keep candidate solutions on the same criteria rather than awarding one option points for an advantage the other option was never assessed against.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A preferred option does not become a supported recommendation merely because it is given a score. Evaluate every candidate against the same criteria and weights, calculate the totals, and explain the recommendation in those terms rather than using an unstructured preference.

video_need.reason: A comparison table can link criterion scores, weighted totals, and the reason for a recommendation.

media.group_title: Compare solution options and explain the recommendation

segments.label: Compare options using shared criteria, weighted scores, and justified trade-offs
segments.summary: A car-selection example introduces a comparison table with shared criteria and a common 1–5 performance scale. Higher scores mean better performance against the criterion: a high cost score means inexpensive, not a higher purchase price. The example first adds unweighted scores, then introduces importance weights because criteria need not matter equally. Each option’s criterion score is multiplied by that criterion’s weight, and the weighted scores are summed. The resulting totals are 75, 55, and 35, supporting the highest-scoring option under that assessment. A facilities-management supplier example then explains a trade-off: although cost has the greatest importance, an option with a poorer cost score can lead overall because of stronger service and easier termination. A supported recommendation considers all agreed criteria and their weights rather than choosing solely on price.

bridge_note.before: Watch how shared criteria become weighted totals and how the supplier recommendation explains a trade-off. The clip calls this a weighted decision matrix; interpret its highest-scoring option as preferred under the chosen assessment.
bridge_note.after: The clip covers shared criteria, weighted calculations, and a criteria-based recommendation. Devspace’s text applies the same method to instruction-access solutions; a higher total supports that assessment’s recommendation, not a guarantee of implementation success.

practice_anchor.objective: Score instruction-access Solutions A and B against three supplied criteria: instruction clarity, fit with agreed operating constraints, and support for the agreed instruction-access need. Use the supplied criterion descriptions, candidate information, common score scale, and importance weights. Multiply scores by weights, sum each solution’s weighted scores, and recommend one.
practice_anchor.success: Both solutions are scored against the same three criteria using the supplied scale. Each weighted score equals its criterion score multiplied by the corresponding weight, totals are correct, and the recommendation explains how the criteria and scores support the choice.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make shared criteria, importance weights, Solutions A and B’s scores, weighted scores, and candidate totals visible together, with the recommendation linked to the criteria that explain the result.

teaching_notes: Avoid claims that scores guarantee implementation success.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

coverage.learning_objective: Learner can develop a business case with cost-benefit analysis justifying a proposed initiative.

required_facts.statement: A business case justifies an initiative by describing the problem, possible solutions, expected benefits, and costs.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/business-case — What is a business case?; Key elements of a business case

required_facts.statement: List and estimate relevant costs and benefits over the period being evaluated, including direct and indirect effects.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/strategic-planning/cost-benefit-analysis — Key components of a cost-benefit analysis

required_facts.statement: Present the recommendation with the supporting financial assessment in the business case.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/business-case — Key elements of a business case

required_facts.statement: For a monetary-return estimate, calculate projected net return = total projected monetary benefits over the evaluation period − project cost, including the cost of the project itself rather than reporting gross savings alone.
source_refs: nngroup_articles#https://www.nngroup.com/articles/calculating-roi-design-projects/ — Step 3: Convert the UX Metric into the KPI; Step 4: Report Responsibly — Example: Health-Insurance Website

required_facts.statement: Interpret a positive projected monetary return as estimated benefits exceeding cost over that period, and report the assumptions and time horizon because the return is an estimate, not a promised financial outcome.
Calculate percentage ROI = (monetary benefits − costs) / costs × 100%, using net monetary return as the numerator and investment cost as the denominator.
source_refs: https://corporatefinanceinstitute.com/resources/accounting/return-on-investment-roi-formula/#ROI Formula; Is there an Excel formula for ROI?

required_facts.statement: Use the costs and monetary benefits for the stated evaluation period, include relevant costs rather than just a headline purchase cost, and use the same time period when comparing alternatives.
source_refs: https://corporatefinanceinstitute.com/resources/accounting/return-on-investment-roi-formula/#Limitations of the ROI Formula; Common Mistakes in Calculating ROI
atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/strategic-planning/cost-benefit-analysis — Key components of a cost-benefit analysis; Identify the costs and benefits

required_facts.statement: Net monetary return is the benefits-minus-costs amount in money, whereas percentage ROI expresses that net return relative to investment cost.
source_refs: https://corporatefinanceinstitute.com/resources/accounting/return-on-investment-roi-formula/#ROI Formula; What is the ROI percentage?

teaching_blocks.content: Imagine a business case for improving delivery-instruction access. Describe the dispatch problem, possible solutions, and expected benefits and costs. For this hypothetical one-year assessment, estimated monetary benefits are 18,000 and relevant project costs total 12,000, including implementation and other relevant costs rather than only a headline purchase price.

teaching_blocks.title: Business Case Development
teaching_blocks.content: A business case justifies an initiative by describing the problem, possible solutions, expected benefits, and costs.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: List and estimate relevant costs and benefits over the period being evaluated, including direct and indirect effects. Present the recommendation with the supporting financial assessment in the business case. For a monetary-return estimate, calculate projected net return = total projected monetary benefits over the evaluation period − project cost, including the cost of the project itself rather than reporting gross savings alone. Interpret a positive projected monetary return as estimated benefits exceeding cost over that period, and report the assumptions and time horizon because the return is an estimate, not a promised financial outcome. Calculate percentage ROI = (monetary benefits − costs) / costs × 100%, using net monetary return as the numerator and investment cost as the denominator. Use the costs and monetary benefits for the stated evaluation period, include relevant costs rather than just a headline purchase cost, and use the same time period when comparing alternatives. Net monetary return is the benefits-minus-costs amount in money, whereas percentage ROI expresses that net return relative to investment cost.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Projected net monetary return is benefits minus costs: 18,000 − 12,000 = 6,000. Percentage ROI is that net return divided by investment cost, times 100%: 6,000 / 12,000 × 100% = 50%. The 6,000 amount and 50% percentage describe different things. Gross benefits of 18,000 are not the net return.

A positive projected monetary return means the estimated benefits exceed cost over the stated period. Report the one-year horizon and the assumptions behind the estimates; this is not a promised financial outcome. If another alternative is compared, use costs and monetary benefits for the same evaluation period, including relevant direct and indirect effects.

Present the recommendation with its supporting financial assessment in the business case. Do not let the calculation replace the problem and option descriptions. The useful output explains why the initiative is being considered and what estimated return supports the recommendation, with the costs, period, and assumptions visible to readers.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: ROI’s numerator is net monetary return, not gross savings. Its denominator is investment cost, not benefits. A positive projection is an estimate under stated assumptions and a time horizon, not a promise. Net return in money and percentage ROI must not be labeled interchangeably.

video_need.reason: Tracing costs and benefits into net return and percentage ROI makes denominators, units, and time horizons clear.

segments.summary: The example recommends developing an admissions website in-house so students can submit and track applications, view admission status, and communicate with admissions staff. It considers doing nothing and making minor portal improvements, explaining that the larger initiative offers greater financial and operational benefits and better addresses the identified issues. The recommendation includes a five-year financial assessment covering operational and development costs. Development estimates should draw on IT expertise, while financial analysts can help estimate tangible and intangible costs.

bridge_note.before: Watch how the admissions website recommendation connects alternatives, expected benefits, and a five-year financial assessment. Its situation and evaluation period differ from our delivery-instruction example.
bridge_note.after: The text supplies the complete justification framework, direct and indirect effects, same-period comparisons, and assumptions. It also teaches the net-return and percentage ROI calculations absent from this clip.

practice_anchor.success: The submitted business case includes the problem, possible solutions, costs, benefits, one-year horizon, and assumptions. It distinguishes the monetary amount from the percentage, describes the positive return as an estimate rather than a promise, and connects the recommendation to the financial assessment. Any alternative comparison uses the same evaluation period.

teaching_notes: Keep cost completeness, same-period comparisons, and estimates explicit; no unsupported NPV or payback formulas.

coverage.learning_objective: Learner can apply multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA) to compare options against several non-comparable dimensions systematically.

required_facts.statement: A decision matrix enables comparison across several criteria using explicit importance weights and scores.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/software/confluence/templates/decision-matrix — What is a decision matrix template?

required_facts.statement: Define criteria and importance weights, then map each criterion’s performance values to a common rating scale with criterion-specific scoring definitions applied consistently to all options and higher ratings meaning better performance.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/software/confluence/templates/decision-matrix — What is a decision matrix template?; Define decision criteria; Score each option against each criterion

required_facts.statement: Calculate each option’s total by multiplying its common-scale rating for each criterion by that criterion’s weight and summing these weighted ratings, rather than raw values in incompatible units, then compare totals for a defensible ranking.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/software/confluence/templates/decision-matrix — Calculate the weighted scores and make a decision

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose two instruction-access options differ in cost and clarity. Cost is measured in money, while clarity uses a rating. Adding 8,000 directly to a clarity score of 4 would mix incompatible units, so define a common rating scale first.

teaching_blocks.title: Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis
teaching_blocks.content: A decision matrix enables comparison across several criteria using explicit importance weights and scores.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Define criteria and importance weights, then map each criterion’s performance values to a common rating scale with criterion-specific scoring definitions applied consistently to all options and higher ratings meaning better performance. Calculate each option’s total by multiplying its common-scale rating for each criterion by that criterion’s weight and summing these weighted ratings, rather than raw values in incompatible units, then compare totals for a defensible ranking.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
For this hypothetical matrix, clarity already uses 1 to 5, with higher ratings better. Define cost ratings specifically: 8,000 maps to 5 and 12,000 maps to 3 for the example options, because lower cost is better under the chosen scoring definitions. Apply each criterion’s definition consistently to every option. Assign weights 0.4 to cost and 0.6 to clarity.

Option A has cost rating 5 and clarity 3, totaling 5 × 0.4 + 3 × 0.6 = 3.8. Option B has cost rating 3 and clarity 5, totaling 3 × 0.4 + 5 × 0.6 = 4.2. Compare those totals for the ranking.

The useful output makes criteria, importance, criterion-specific scoring definitions, and weighted totals explicit. The invented mappings are part of this assessment, not a universal monetary conversion. Higher ratings must mean better performance across the criteria, including cost, so the weighted sum has a consistent interpretation.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Weights do not make incompatible raw units directly comparable. Map performance to a common rating scale with criterion-specific definitions first. Also reverse the scoring direction where needed so higher ratings mean better performance rather than accidentally rewarding higher cost.

video_need.reason: Mapping different units to a common scale before calculating weighted totals benefits from a worked matrix.

media.group_title: Compare options with a weighted decision matrix

segments.label: Rank conference venues using criteria, importance weights, and common-scale ratings
segments.summary: Four potential conference venues are compared using location, facilities, and cost. Location and facilities are divided into more detailed criteria. The example assigns first-level importance weights of 0.35, 0.45, and 0.20, with separate weights within each detailed group. Performance ratings use a scale where 100 represents the best performance and zero the worst. For venue A, environment and transportation ratings of zero and 100 receive equal weights, producing a location rating of 50. That rating is multiplied by the location weight of 0.35 and combined with the other weighted ratings to produce an overall total of 48.8. The resulting totals place B first, followed by D, A, and C. Comparing their performance also reveals trade-offs: B scores highest but is expensive, while C is inexpensive but performs poorly overall. The ranking supports a decision based on what matters to stakeholders; it does not make the highest-scoring option an automatic choice.

bridge_note.before: Watch how common-scale performance ratings and importance weights produce venue totals. The clip uses two levels of criteria; focus on the same multiply-and-sum principle taught in the text.
bridge_note.after: The clip compares weighted totals but does not establish explicit criterion-specific scoring definitions for all performance values. The text supplies that missing step so ratings can be applied consistently.

practice_anchor.objective: Rank three hypothetical instruction-access options across three criteria measured in non-comparable units. Use supplied performance values and criterion-specific scoring definitions to assign common-scale ratings, choose and state importance weights, and calculate weighted totals using ordinary arithmetic.
practice_anchor.success: All three options are rated using the same supplied definition for each criterion, with higher ratings consistently meaning better performance. Each total sums ratings multiplied by their criterion weights rather than incompatible raw values. The options are ordered from highest to lowest total, with the ranking justified by the stated weights, scoring definitions, and calculations.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make a three-option, three-criterion decision matrix visible, showing raw performance values and units, criterion-specific scoring definitions, common-scale ratings, importance weights, weighted contributions, totals, and the resulting ranking.

teaching_notes: No invented normalization formula; use explicitly defined sample ratings.

coverage.learning_objective: Learner can compute and choose among mean, median, and mode to describe a dataset's central tendency.

required_facts.statement: The sample mean is computed as the sum of the observed values divided by the number of observations.
The median is the middle value when the data are ordered from smallest to largest; if there is an even number of observations, the median is the average of the two middle values.
The mode is the value that occurs most often in the data; there can be more than one mode.

The mean is more strongly affected by extreme observations (such as those in the tail of a skewed distribution) than the median, which is more robust to them; for this reason the median can better represent a typical value in a skewed dataset.

teaching_blocks.content: Imagine five observed dispatch-preparation times in minutes: 2, 3, 3, 4, and 18. The mean is the sum divided by the number of observations: 30 / 5 = 6 minutes. The ordered middle value is 3, so the median is 3 minutes. The most frequent value is also 3, so the mode is 3 minutes.

teaching_blocks.title: Descriptive Measures Of Center
teaching_blocks.content: The sample mean is computed as the sum of the observed values divided by the number of observations.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: The median is the middle value when the data are ordered from smallest to largest; if there is an even number of observations, the median is the average of the two middle values. The mode is the value that occurs most often in the data; there can be more than one mode. The mean is more strongly affected by extreme observations (such as those in the tail of a skewed distribution) than the median, which is more robust to them; for this reason the median can better represent a typical value in a skewed dataset.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
The extreme 18-minute observation affects the mean more strongly than the median. In this skewed sample, the median can better represent a typical value than the mean. Do not hide the extreme observation; explain why the two center summaries differ.

For an even-sized example, 2, 3, 4, and 9 has median (3 + 4) / 2 = 3.5. For mode, 2, 2, 4, and 4 has two most frequent values, so both 2 and 4 are modes. These examples apply the definitions rather than assuming every dataset has a single mode or a median that is an observed value.

The practical BA task is to interpret a center measure in the context of the business data. A report saying “average preparation time is 6 minutes” should be clear that it uses the mean. The median answers a different center question and is more robust to extreme observations.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Mean, median, and mode are not interchangeable names for one number. Order values before finding the median, average the two middle values when the count is even, and allow multiple modes. An extreme value can pull the mean away from the median.

video_need.reason: Ordering values and changing an extreme observation makes center measures and their sensitivity visible.

practice_anchor.objective: Order the hypothetical dispatch-preparation times 2, 3, 3, 4, and 18 minutes; compute their mean, median, and mode using arithmetic; and justify which best represents a typical preparation time. Also find the median for 2, 3, 4, and 9 minutes and all modes for 2, 2, 4, and 4 minutes.
practice_anchor.success: The learner obtains a mean of 6 minutes, a median of 3 minutes, and a mode of 3 minutes for the five observations. They justify choosing the median for a typical preparation time because the extreme 18-minute observation affects the mean more strongly, without discarding that observation. They obtain 3.5 minutes for the even-sized median example and identify both 2 and 4 minutes as modes in the tied-frequency example.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show the dispatch-preparation observations in ascending order, with their sum and count, middle position or positions, and repeated values marked. Make the mean of 6 minutes and median of 3 minutes visible beside the extreme 18-minute observation; include the even-count and multiple-mode examples.

teaching_notes: Do not introduce inferential statistics or automatic outlier removal.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

coverage.learning_objective: Learner can compute and interpret range, variance, and standard deviation to describe a dataset's spread.

required_facts.statement: The range of a data set is the largest value minus the smallest value.

The variance is computed by taking each observation's deviation from the mean, squaring it, summing the squared deviations, and dividing by n - 1 (one less than the number of observations); it is roughly the average squared distance of the observations from the mean.
The standard deviation is the square root of the variance, and it describes the typical distance of an observation from the mean.

The standard deviation is expressed in the same units as the original data, while the variance is expressed in squared units; the range is based only on the two most extreme values and ignores how the rest of the data are spread.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose dispatch-preparation times are 2, 4, and 6 minutes. Their mean is 4. The range is 6 − 2 = 4 minutes. For the sample variance, subtract the mean from each observation to get -2, 0, and 2; square these deviations to get 4, 0, and 4; then sum to 8.

teaching_blocks.title: Measures Of Spread
teaching_blocks.content: The range of a data set is the largest value minus the smallest value.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: The variance is computed by taking each observation's deviation from the mean, squaring it, summing the squared deviations, and dividing by n - 1 (one less than the number of observations); it is roughly the average squared distance of the observations from the mean. The standard deviation is the square root of the variance, and it describes the typical distance of an observation from the mean. The standard deviation is expressed in the same units as the original data, while the variance is expressed in squared units; the range is based only on the two most extreme values and ignores how the rest of the data are spread.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Divide by n − 1, which is 2 for three observations: variance is 8 / 2 = 4 square minutes. Standard deviation is the square root of that variance, or 2 minutes. The different units matter: variance is squared, while standard deviation uses the original minutes and describes typical distance from the mean.

Range only uses the smallest and largest values. A second sample, 2, 4, 4, 4, and 6, has the same range, but its variance is 8 / 4 = 2 square minutes and standard deviation is about 1.41 minutes. The added central observations change the spread calculation without changing the extremes.

The practical reporting point is that range alone does not describe how the rest of the data are spread. State which measure you use and its units. The variance formula here is the sample form with n − 1; keep that denominator instead of silently switching to another convention.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Do not divide this sample-variance calculation by n: the stated denominator is n − 1. Standard deviation is not the variance itself, and it is not in squared units. Equal ranges also do not prove equal spread among all observations.

video_need.reason: Tracing deviations, squares, denominator, and square root makes the calculation and units concrete.

practice_anchor.objective: Use arithmetic to compute the range, sample variance, and standard deviation for dispatch-preparation times of 2, 4, and 6 minutes, then compare their consistency with times of 2, 4, 4, 4, and 6 minutes.
practice_anchor.success: Obtain a range of 4 minutes for both samples. Using squared deviations from the mean and the n − 1 denominator, obtain sample variances of 4 and 2 square minutes and standard deviations of 2 and approximately 1.41 minutes, respectively. Explain that both means are 4 minutes, but the second sample has less spread around the mean and is more consistent despite the equal ranges.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make each sample's observations, mean, deviations, squared deviations, and squared-deviation sum visible alongside its n − 1 denominator, sample variance in square minutes, standard deviation in minutes, and range. Show that the samples have equal means and ranges but different standard deviations.

teaching_notes: Explicitly label sample variance; examples have at least two observations.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

coverage.learning_objective: Learner can write and refine user stories following INVEST criteria, including splitting oversized stories.

required_facts.statement: A user story states a persona’s need and its purpose using “As a [persona], I [want to], [so that].”
Refine oversized backlog items by breaking them into smaller, more precise items with clearer descriptions.
Split larger stories into smaller stories that can be completed within an iteration.
Use INVEST as a quality checklist for each rewritten or split story; if a criterion fails, consider rewording or rewriting the story.
Independent means stories should not overlap in concept and should be schedulable and implementable in any order; check whether a story can be implemented without requiring another story first.
Negotiable means a story captures the essential need rather than a fixed contract of feature details; check that details can be worked out collaboratively with the customer.
Valuable means a story delivers value to the customer; check that each split story describes a customer-valued result rather than only a technical layer.
Estimable means the team can approximate the work well enough to rank and schedule it; check that the team understands the story and its scope well enough to make an estimate.
Small means a story fits within an iteration; check the size of each proposed story and split work that cannot fit.
Testable means the desired result is clear enough to write a test for it; check that the customer can describe how to verify the story, and clarify stories whose result cannot be tested.

teaching_blocks.content: Imagine a backlog story saying, “As a dispatcher, I want all order-management capabilities, so that I can do my work.” It is broad enough that the team cannot clearly discuss its scope or finish it within an iteration. Refinement breaks oversized items into smaller, more precise stories.

teaching_blocks.title: User Story Writing and Refinement
teaching_blocks.content: A user story states a persona’s need and its purpose using “As a [persona], I [want to], [so that].”

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Refine oversized backlog items by breaking them into smaller, more precise items with clearer descriptions. Split larger stories into smaller stories that can be completed within an iteration. Use INVEST as a quality checklist for each rewritten or split story; if a criterion fails, consider rewording or rewriting the story. Independent means stories should not overlap in concept and should be schedulable and implementable in any order; check whether a story can be implemented without requiring another story first. Negotiable means a story captures the essential need rather than a fixed contract of feature details; check that details can be worked out collaboratively with the customer. Valuable means a story delivers value to the customer; check that each split story describes a customer-valued result rather than only a technical layer. Estimable means the team can approximate the work well enough to rank and schedule it; check that the team understands the story and its scope well enough to make an estimate. Small means a story fits within an iteration; check the size of each proposed story and split work that cannot fit. Testable means the desired result is clear enough to write a test for it; check that the customer can describe how to verify the story, and clarify stories whose result cannot be tested.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
For this hypothetical case, rewrite one story around seeing current instructions and another around finding orders by customer. Each needs a persona’s need and purpose, not merely a technical layer. Check each rewritten story with INVEST. Independent asks whether it can be implemented without requiring the other first and without conceptual overlap. Negotiable asks whether it captures the essential need while details remain open to collaboration. Valuable asks whether it delivers a customer-valued result.

Estimable asks whether the team understands it well enough to approximate the work for ranking and scheduling. Small asks whether it fits within an iteration. Testable asks whether the customer can describe how to verify the result. If the rewritten instruction story still says only “make access better,” clarify it until a test can be described. If it cannot fit, split it further.

The output is not just more story cards. It is a set of clearer, smaller stories checked for all six qualities. The example split is a candidate to assess, not a guarantee of independence or size without the team’s checks.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Splitting into “database,” “interface,” and “testing” pieces does not by itself satisfy Valuable: each split story should describe a customer-valued result. Nor does using the story sentence format prove INVEST is met. Check each quality and reword or rewrite failures.

video_need.reason: The distinction and the worked business example can be understood from prose; one simple annotated visual is sufficient and a motion demonstration would mostly repeat the text.

practice_anchor.objective: Split the oversized dispatcher story about all order-management capabilities into two or three smaller stories, using the hypothetical needs of seeing current instructions and finding orders by customer. Write each in the persona–need–purpose format and assess each against all six INVEST criteria.
practice_anchor.success: Submit two or three precise stories, each expressing a persona, need, and customer-valued purpose, together with an INVEST check for each. Check conceptual overlap and whether either story requires another first; keep details negotiable; explain customer value, scope clarity for estimation, iteration fit, and how the customer could verify the result. Reword or split any identified failures, and identify assumptions needing team or customer confirmation rather than declaring independence or iteration fit without support.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show the oversized dispatcher story alongside two or three candidate smaller stories. Annotate each candidate's persona, need, and purpose, and display the six INVEST checks, distinguishing supported qualities from assumptions that still require confirmation.

teaching_notes: Include all INVEST meanings; do not assume an invented split is automatically independent.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

coverage.learning_objective: Learner can maintain and groom a product backlog: ordering, refining, and keeping items ready for upcoming sprints.

required_facts.statement: A product backlog is an emergent, ordered list of work needed to improve the product.
Refinement breaks items into smaller, more precise items and adds details such as description, order, and size.
Review unclear or oversized items, clarify their details, split them as needed, and keep the backlog ordered.
Items that can be completed within one iteration are ready for selection; refinement usually provides the needed transparency.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose the order-service backlog contains a broad instruction-access item, a clearer customer-search item, and an outdated vague item called “reporting improvements.” The product backlog is an emergent ordered list of needed product-improvement work, not a fixed archive of every initial idea.

teaching_blocks.title: Backlog Management
teaching_blocks.content: A product backlog is an emergent, ordered list of work needed to improve the product.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Refinement breaks items into smaller, more precise items and adds details such as description, order, and size. Review unclear or oversized items, clarify their details, split them as needed, and keep the backlog ordered. Items that can be completed within one iteration are ready for selection; refinement usually provides the needed transparency.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Refine unclear or oversized items. For the instruction item, clarify the description and break it into smaller, more precise items if needed. For the vague reporting item, establish the intended detail before treating it as ready. Add detail such as description, order, and size, then keep the backlog ordered.

Items that can be completed within one iteration are ready for selection; refinement usually provides the transparency needed for that judgment. Do not label an oversized item ready merely because it appears near the top. Conversely, refinement is not just changing order: it also improves detail and precision.

The useful BA contribution is clearer items and an understandable ordered backlog. Keep clarification, splitting, detail, and ordering visible rather than treating the backlog as a static archive.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A backlog is not simply an unordered requirements list. Refinement also does more than re-rank items: it makes them smaller and more precise with relevant details. High placement alone does not establish that an item fits within an iteration.

video_need.reason: The distinction and the worked business example can be understood from prose; one simple annotated visual is sufficient and a motion demonstration would mostly repeat the text.

practice_anchor.objective: Refine a messy order-service backlog containing instruction access, customer search, and reporting improvements. Use supplied business priorities and clarification details to reorder items, split oversized work into smaller precise items, add description and size details, and mark refinement status.
practice_anchor.success: The backlog reflects the supplied priorities; unclear items have clarified descriptions or remain marked as needing clarification; oversized items are split as needed; and only sufficiently clear items that can be completed within one iteration are marked ready for selection.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show the order-service backlog before and after refinement, making changes to item order, descriptions, size, splitting, and refinement status visible. Distinguish high placement from readiness for selection.

teaching_notes: Preserve “usually” for refinement transparency; avoid assigning later Scrum accountabilities prematurely.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

coverage.learning_objective: Learner can sequence prioritized requirements into delivery phases/releases based on priority, dependency, and capacity.

required_facts.statement: A roadmap sequences planned work against goals rather than listing disconnected features.
Group planned initiatives into a sequence such as Now, Next, and Later, linking the sequence to goals and tracking dependencies.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management/roadmaps — Who is responsible for the product roadmap?; roadmap examples; Tips and tricks

required_facts.statement: Review the sequence as priorities and information change rather than treating the initial roadmap as fixed.

teaching_blocks.content: Imagine planned order-service work includes current-instruction access, a customer-search improvement, and broader multi-branch reporting. A roadmap sequences planned work against goals rather than presenting disconnected features.

teaching_blocks.title: Phased Delivery Sequencing
teaching_blocks.content: A roadmap sequences planned work against goals rather than listing disconnected features.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Group planned initiatives into a sequence such as Now, Next, and Later, linking the sequence to goals and tracking dependencies. Review the sequence as priorities and information change rather than treating the initial roadmap as fixed.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
For this hypothetical roadmap, place instruction access in Now to support the dispatch-preparation goal, customer search in Next to support faster order finding, and multi-branch reporting in Later to support branch comparison. Track known dependencies as part of the sequence. If later reporting depends on agreed branch information, make that connection visible instead of treating the three labels as independent wish lists.

Now, Next, and Later are an example sequence, not fixed dates promised by this concept. Link each initiative to its goal so a stakeholder can understand why it occupies that part of the roadmap. Then review the sequence as priorities and information change.

If new information changes which work supports the immediate goal, reconsider the initial placement. The useful output is goal-linked planned sequencing with dependencies and revision, not a permanent commitment disguised as a diagram. The example initiatives are invented for the exercise; their particular order is not a universal rule for BA delivery.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A roadmap is not just a list of features with three headings. The sequence should connect to goals and track dependencies. Also, the initial sequence is not fixed: review it as priorities and information change rather than claiming the first roadmap cannot be revised.

video_need.reason: A goal-linked sequence with dependency cues can make the relationship between initiatives and phases easier to follow.

media.group_title: Goal-linked releases that change with learning

segments.label: Sequence releases around goals and revise them as information changes
segments.summary: An online bookstore example groups planned work into releases with different goals. The first release supports validation through a basic end-to-end flow: a home page, title search, adding a book to a shopping cart, and credit-card checkout. A second release aims toward public availability by adding categories, book details, and removal from the cart. If learning shows that customers will not pay by credit card, cash on delivery moves into the second release. Other additions are deferred: further stakeholder-requested features are considered for release three, while PayPal checkout and buying multiple copies of a book are considered for release four. These placements illustrate a sequence that changes with new information, not a universal release plan.

bridge_note.before: Watch how the bookstore example links releases to validation and public availability, then changes the sequence when payment preferences become clearer. Its numbered releases illustrate sequencing rather than fixed dates.
bridge_note.after: The clip illustrates goal-linked sequencing and revision. It does not fully teach grouping initiatives into Now, Next, and Later with explicit dependency tracking; the text covers that missing element.

practice_anchor.objective: Sequence 10 prioritized requirements from the hypothetical order-service situation into three releases, using supplied goals and dependencies to justify their placement.
practice_anchor.success: All 10 requirements are assigned to three goal-linked releases. Each prerequisite is placed before the work that depends on it, including an explicit internal order if both share a release. Placement reflects the supplied priorities without treating release labels as fixed dates.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the three-release sequence visible, with all 10 requirements grouped by release, each release linked to its goal, and dependency arrows showing prerequisite order.

teaching_notes: Do not invent scheduling authority or fixed durations for Now/Next/Later.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

coverage.learning_objective: Learner can collaboratively define testable acceptance criteria for a backlog item during refinement, establishing what 'done' means.

required_facts.statement: Acceptance criteria state the conditions used to determine whether a particular user story is satisfied.
Discuss what completing the story means, make the acceptance conditions testable, and document that shared understanding.
source_refs: atlassian_user_stories#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/project-management/user-stories — How to write user stories — Definition of done; What is in a user story?

required_facts.statement: Refinement adds detail to make backlog items more precise and understandable.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose a story says dispatchers want to see current instructions so they can prepare the correct order. Acceptance criteria state the conditions used to judge whether this particular story is satisfied. Discuss what completing it means instead of relying only on the story’s short wording.

teaching_blocks.title: Acceptance Criteria Definition
teaching_blocks.content: Acceptance criteria state the conditions used to determine whether a particular user story is satisfied.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Discuss what completing the story means, make the acceptance conditions testable, and document that shared understanding. Refinement adds detail to make backlog items more precise and understandable.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
For this hypothetical case, the stakeholders agree that selecting an existing order displays its current instructions, and selecting an unknown identifier displays a not-found result. Make those acceptance conditions testable and document the shared understanding. “The lookup is good” does not describe a clear completion condition.

During refinement, add detail that makes the backlog item more precise and understandable. If stakeholders disagree about what “current” means, clarify that point before leaving the criterion as if everyone interpreted it identically. The example conditions are agreed choices for this story, not a complete checklist for all instruction-access systems.

The useful output is story-specific completion understanding that can be checked. It should connect directly to the desired behavior rather than becoming a broad quality slogan. Keep the conditions in the shared record so later discussion is about the documented understanding, not a different person’s recollection of what was meant.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Acceptance criteria belong to a particular story. They are not a substitute for clarifying what that story means, and vague positive wording does not make them testable. Discuss and document the shared completion conditions instead of assuming the title is sufficient.
