coverage.learning_objective: Learner can collaborate effectively as a BA with the Product Owner and delivery team across the sprint cycle.

required_facts.statement: The Product Owner is accountable for maximizing product value and effective backlog management.
The Product Owner may delegate backlog-management work but remains accountable for it.
Developers are responsible for sizing the work and deciding how selected work is performed.
Clarify backlog items collaboratively while respecting the Product Owner’s ordering accountability and the Developers’ delivery decisions.
source_refs: scrum_guide#https://scrumguides.org/scrum-guide.html — Product Owner; Product Backlog; Sprint Planning

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose the BA is helping clarify an instruction-access item while the Product Owner and Developers discuss delivery. Product Owner accountability includes maximizing product value and effective backlog management. Some backlog-management work can be delegated, but that does not transfer the accountability.

teaching_blocks.title: Product Owner and Team Collaboration
teaching_blocks.content: The Product Owner is accountable for maximizing product value and effective backlog management.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: The Product Owner may delegate backlog-management work but remains accountable for it. Developers are responsible for sizing the work and deciding how selected work is performed. Clarify backlog items collaboratively while respecting the Product Owner’s ordering accountability and the Developers’ delivery decisions.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
In this hypothetical collaboration, the BA drafts clearer item wording and brings stakeholder questions to the group. The Product Owner remains accountable for ordering. Developers size the work and decide how selected work will be performed. The BA’s useful contribution is clarification that helps these decisions, not taking them over.

If a stakeholder asks the BA to promise a size or dictate the implementation approach, distinguish the BA’s requirements contribution from Developers' responsibility. If the BA updates backlog detail under delegated work, distinguish doing that task from becoming accountable for product value and backlog management.

The practical mental model is collaboration with explicit boundaries. People can contribute to the same item while retaining different accountabilities and delivery decisions. Clear descriptions support collaboration, but they should not be presented as authority to impose order, size, or implementation on the people accountable for those decisions.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Delegating backlog-management work does not transfer the Product Owner’s accountability. Nor does preparing requirements make the BA responsible for sizing or deciding how selected work is performed. Collaborate on clarity while respecting ordering and delivery boundaries.

video_need.reason: The distinction and the worked business example can be understood from prose; one simple annotated visual is sufficient and a motion demonstration would mostly repeat the text.

practice_anchor.objective: Resolve role ambiguity in the hypothetical instruction-access item by matching proposed actions to the appropriate role: BA clarification, Product Owner accountability for product value and backlog management including ordering, or Developers' responsibility for sizing and implementation decisions.
practice_anchor.success: The matches form a collaboration approach in which the BA drafts clearer wording and brings stakeholder questions, the Product Owner retains accountability even when backlog-management tasks are delegated, and Developers size the work and decide how selected work is performed.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the collaboration boundaries visible around the instruction-access item: BA contributions clarify requirements, Product Owner accountability covers product value and backlog management including ordering, and Developers own sizing and decisions about how selected work is performed. Annotate delegated backlog work to show that accountability remains with the Product Owner.

teaching_notes: Do not conflate BA contribution with Product Owner or Developer authority.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

coverage.learning_objective: Learner can participate in the daily standup as a BA, surfacing blockers relevant to requirements/clarification without turning it into a status meeting.

required_facts.statement: The Daily Scrum is a 15-minute event for Developers focused on progress toward the Sprint Goal and an actionable plan.
Participation by other Scrum accountabilities as Developers depends on actively working on iteration backlog items.
Give an update that identifies an impediment or needed coordination affecting the goal and the next work plan.
Move detailed replanning discussion outside the Daily Scrum rather than extending the event.

teaching_blocks.content: The Daily Scrum is a 15-minute event for Developers focused on progress toward the Sprint Goal and an actionable plan. Other Scrum accountabilities participate as Developers when actively working on iteration backlog items. For example: “The instruction clarification blocks this goal-related item; I need coordination to resolve it, then continue the planned work.” Keep detailed replanning outside the event rather than extending it.

video_need.reason: The distinction and the worked business example can be understood from prose; one simple annotated visual is sufficient and a motion demonstration would mostly repeat the text.

practice_anchor.objective: Write a brief Daily Scrum update for the hypothetical situation in which an instruction clarification blocks a goal-related backlog item. Identify the impediment, needed coordination, and next work plan.
practice_anchor.success: The update connects the clarification blocker to the Sprint Goal, states the coordination needed to resolve it, and identifies the work to continue afterward. It leaves detailed replanning outside the 15-minute event rather than becoming a detailed status report.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show two updates for the same instruction-clarification scenario: a concise update annotated with goal impact, blocker, needed coordination, and next work plan; and a detailed status report annotated to identify discussion that belongs outside the Daily Scrum.

teaching_notes: Keep brief; no automatic BA attendance rule.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

coverage.learning_objective: Learner can participate in sprint review as a BA, helping validate delivered work against acceptance criteria with stakeholders.

required_facts.statement: The Sprint Review inspects the outcome with stakeholders and determines future adaptations; it is a working session rather than just a presentation.
Acceptance criteria provide the story-specific conditions used to judge whether delivered behavior satisfies the need.
Compare the demonstrated behavior with those conditions and discuss differences with the stakeholders.

teaching_blocks.content: Imagine stakeholders examining the iteration’s order-service outcome. The Sprint Review is a working session for inspecting that outcome and determining future adaptations, not merely a polished presentation.

teaching_blocks.title: Sprint Review (BA Involvement)
teaching_blocks.content: The Sprint Review inspects the outcome with stakeholders and determines future adaptations; it is a working session rather than just a presentation.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Acceptance criteria provide the story-specific conditions used to judge whether delivered behavior satisfies the need. Compare the demonstrated behavior with those conditions and discuss differences with the stakeholders.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
For this hypothetical story, acceptance conditions say that selecting an existing order displays current instructions and an unknown identifier displays a not-found result. Compare the demonstrated behavior with those story-specific conditions. If the unknown-identifier case behaves differently, discuss that difference with stakeholders rather than relying on a general claim that the demo looked successful.

Use the inspection to discuss future adaptations. The conditions help judge whether the demonstrated behavior satisfies the particular need, while the review addresses the outcome with stakeholders. Keep the example’s conditions visible so participants can connect what they saw with what was expected.

The useful BA contribution is evidence-based comparison and discussion of differences. Use the inspection for collaborative adaptation rather than treating the event as a one-way show.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A presentation of features alone does not capture the review’s working-session purpose. Compare behavior with the story’s acceptance conditions and discuss differences with stakeholders. A convincing demonstration is not evidence that every specified condition was met.

video_need.reason: A review example can show demonstrated behavior compared with conditions and discussed as future adaptations.

media.group_title: Sprint Review: inspection, feedback, and adaptation

segments.label: Inspect the outcome and make room for stakeholder feedback
segments.summary: A Sprint Review brings participants, including real end users, together to inspect delivered work and adapt based on what they discover. The example concerns an improved table component for creating and editing broadcasting work orders. The narrator points out that the Product Owner is enthusiastic about showing completed work but has not left enough room for feedback. A demonstration is only the beginning of a review: it should trigger stakeholder feedback rather than end the discussion.

bridge_note.before: Watch how the work-order example distinguishes showing delivered work from inviting feedback. The clip uses “increment” for the delivered outcome that participants inspect together.
bridge_note.after: The clip establishes inspection and feedback, but does not explain acceptance criteria or compare behavior against them. The text supplies those story-specific conditions and explains how to discuss mismatches.

practice_anchor.objective: Compare supplied demonstration observations for the hypothetical order-service feature with its acceptance criteria: an existing order displays current instructions, and an unknown identifier displays a not-found result. Select any mismatched observations and identify the corresponding unmet criterion.
practice_anchor.success: Correctly distinguish matching behavior from mismatches, associate each mismatch with its original acceptance criterion, and identify the difference to raise with stakeholders.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show the hypothetical order-service acceptance criteria beside the corresponding demonstrated behavior, with mismatches clearly marked for stakeholder discussion.

teaching_notes: Do not introduce Definition of Done rules before their concept; keep review focused on inspection and adaptation.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

coverage.learning_objective: Learner can participate in a sprint retrospective as a BA, contributing to identifying process improvements for the team.

required_facts.statement: The Sprint Retrospective plans ways to improve quality and effectiveness.
Review what went well, what problems occurred, and how they were or were not solved, considering interactions, processes, and tools.
Identify a concrete change that would improve effectiveness and arrange to address the most helpful improvements promptly.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose the team completed an iteration but spent significant effort clarifying instruction wording late in the work. The retrospective plans ways to improve quality and effectiveness; it is not another stakeholder presentation of the product outcome.

teaching_blocks.title: Sprint Retrospective (BA Involvement)
teaching_blocks.content: The Sprint Retrospective plans ways to improve quality and effectiveness.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Review what went well, what problems occurred, and how they were or were not solved, considering interactions, processes, and tools. Identify a concrete change that would improve effectiveness and arrange to address the most helpful improvements promptly.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Review what went well, what problems occurred, and how those problems were or were not solved. In this hypothetical discussion, clear customer examples worked well, while late uncertainty about “current instructions” interrupted work. Consider interactions, processes, and tools rather than treating the issue as only one person’s performance.

Identify a concrete change. The team might agree to clarify instruction examples during refinement and arrange to address that helpful improvement promptly. That is an example action chosen for this situation, not a mandatory retrospective technique.

The useful output is a specific improvement the team intends to address, grounded in its review. A record saying only “communicate better” leaves the change unclear. Keep the discussion connected to what happened and what can improve effectiveness, including whether earlier problems were actually solved. The focus is learning about the team’s way of working, not inventing a new product requirement simply because the team has held a meeting.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A retrospective is not just a list of complaints or a repeat of the Sprint Review. It examines quality and effectiveness and leads toward concrete improvements. Naming a problem without identifying a helpful change does not complete that purpose.

video_need.reason: The distinction and the worked business example can be understood from prose; one simple annotated visual is sufficient and a motion demonstration would mostly repeat the text.

practice_anchor.objective: Record one actionable retrospective improvement for the hypothetical sprint in which clear customer examples worked well but late uncertainty about current instructions interrupted work.
practice_anchor.success: The recorded item identifies a concrete change to the team's way of working, connects it to the described sprint events, explains how it could improve quality or effectiveness, and specifies how the team will arrange to address it promptly rather than merely stating a complaint.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show the connection between the sprint's late instruction uncertainty and a concrete improvement: contrast the vague item 'communicate better' with clarifying instruction examples during refinement and arranging to address that change promptly.

teaching_notes: Avoid unsupported retrospective ceremonies or mandatory voting methods.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

coverage.learning_objective: Learner can apply the Five Whys technique to trace a problem back to its root cause by repeatedly asking why.

required_facts.statement: Five Whys traces a problem’s cause by repeatedly asking why the previous explanation occurred.
Write the problem, ask why it happened, record the answer, and ask why that answer happened to extend the causal chain.
Five is a guide rather than a required stopping point; use the chain to reach an underlying cause rather than restating the symptom.

teaching_blocks.content: Imagine the problem statement is “Dispatch preparation is delayed by clarification calls.” Ask why those calls occurred. In this hypothetical causal chain, staff could not find current instructions. Ask why that happened: amended instructions remained in a separate record. Ask why they remained separate: the handoff did not identify where the current instruction record should be updated.

teaching_blocks.title: Five Whys
teaching_blocks.content: Five Whys traces a problem’s cause by repeatedly asking why the previous explanation occurred.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Write the problem, ask why it happened, record the answer, and ask why that answer happened to extend the causal chain. Five is a guide rather than a required stopping point; use the chain to reach an underlying cause rather than restating the symptom.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Write each answer and use it as the starting point for the next why question. The chain moves from the stated problem toward an underlying cause instead of repeatedly renaming “dispatch delay.” These answers are assumptions provided for the exercise, not a factual diagnosis of a real team’s process.

Five is a guide, not a required stopping point. Do not invent a fifth explanation merely to reach the technique’s name, and do not stop automatically at five if the chain has not reached an underlying cause. Keep the successive explanation visible so a reader can follow how the cause of the previous explanation is being examined.

The useful output is a recorded causal chain tied to the original problem. The technique is not a guarantee that the first plausible answer is the true cause. Repeated why questions should extend the underlying explanation rather than restate the symptom.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: “Why?” followed by the same symptom in different words does not extend the causal chain. Five is not a compulsory count. Avoid manufacturing answers to fill five lines or treating the technique’s name as proof that the fifth answer must be the root cause.

video_need.reason: A drawn question-and-answer chain can show how each why extends the previous explanation.

media.group_title: Five Whys: from symptom to underlying cause

segments.label: Five Whys: trace a machine stoppage to its underlying cause
segments.summary: Five Whys extends a causal chain by asking why each previous explanation occurred. The example traces a machine stoppage through a blown fuse, overload, insufficient bearing lubrication, a pump that fails to draw lubricant, and a worn pump shaft. The underlying cause identified is a missing strainer that allowed metal chips to damage the pump. Following the explanations back toward the stoppage helps check the chain's causal logic. The number of questions is flexible: three or eight may be appropriate if they reach an underlying cause rather than stop at a symptom.

bridge_note.before: Watch how each why builds on the previous explanation in the machine example. The clip also calls Five Whys a causal chain; focus on the connections, not the number of questions.
bridge_note.after: The clip distinguishes an underlying cause from a symptom and makes the question count flexible. It does not teach the written-answer workflow; the text explains how to record and extend the chain.

practice_anchor.objective: Apply Five Whys to the hypothetical dispatch-preparation problem by arranging the supplied causal answers in sequence, recording the why connection between each pair, and stating the underlying cause. (Fact citations: f1, f2, f3.)
practice_anchor.success: The recorded chain proceeds from clarification calls to staff being unable to find current instructions, then to amended instructions remaining in a separate record, and finally to the handoff not identifying where the current instruction record should be updated. The learner states that final explanation as the exercise's underlying cause, distinguishes it from dispatch delay, and does not invent additional answers to reach five.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the hypothetical dispatch causal chain visible, with the original symptom, successive recorded explanations linked by why, and the underlying handoff cause clearly distinguished from the symptom. (Fact citations: f1, f2, f3.)

teaching_notes: All sample causal answers are hypothetical; do not present guesses as verified real causes.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

coverage.learning_objective: Learner can build a fishbone (Ishikawa) diagram organizing candidate causes of a problem into standard categories.

required_facts.statement: A fishbone diagram organizes possible causes of a problem to support root cause analysis.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/software/confluence/templates/fishbone-diagram — What is a fishbone diagram template?

required_facts.statement: Write a specific problem statement, select cause categories appropriate to the problem, and brainstorm potential causes with the team.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/software/confluence/templates/fishbone-diagram — Define the problem; Choose categories; Brainstorm potential causes

required_facts.statement: Place each proposed cause under its category branch to expose patterns; then analyze the proposed causes and agree actions addressing the root cause.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/software/confluence/templates/fishbone-diagram — Organize causes; Analyze the diagram; Develop an action plan

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose the specific problem is “Orders wait for instruction clarification before dispatch.” A fishbone diagram organizes possible causes for analysis rather than declaring every proposed cause proven.

teaching_blocks.title: Fishbone Diagram
teaching_blocks.content: A fishbone diagram organizes possible causes of a problem to support root cause analysis.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Write a specific problem statement, select cause categories appropriate to the problem, and brainstorm potential causes with the team. Place each proposed cause under its category branch to expose patterns; then analyze the proposed causes and agree actions addressing the root cause.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
For this hypothetical team discussion, select categories suited to the problem, such as information, handoffs, and tools. Write the problem statement and brainstorm potential causes. Place “amendments stored separately” under information, “unclear update responsibility” under handoffs, and “difficult instruction lookup” under tools. These category names and causes are example choices, not a mandatory universal set.

Use the branches to expose patterns in the proposed causes. Then analyze them and agree actions addressing the root cause. Do not jump from a busy branch to a causal conclusion without that analysis. The diagram’s organizational role helps the team see possibilities; the later analysis is what examines them.

The useful output is a structured cause discussion connected to a specific problem, followed by analyzed causes and agreed actions. A vague problem such as “everything is slow” gives the branches less focus than a concrete statement about waiting for clarification. Keep potential causes explicitly potential until they have been analyzed rather than labeling the diagram a proof of cause.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Putting a cause on a branch does not verify it. A fishbone diagram organizes possible causes, which still need analysis before actions address the root cause. The categories should suit the problem, not be treated as a fixed set every business must use.

video_need.reason: Drawing category branches and placing proposed causes makes organization and later analysis distinct.

practice_anchor.objective: Build a fishbone diagram for the problem “Orders wait for instruction clarification before dispatch.” Create at least three appropriate category branches and place the candidate causes “amendments stored separately,” “unclear update responsibility,” and “difficult instruction lookup” under suitable branches.
practice_anchor.success: The diagram displays the specific problem, at least three relevant category branches, and each candidate cause on an appropriate branch. For example, information, handoffs, and tools accommodate the three supplied causes respectively. Other suitable category choices are acceptable, and the causes remain labeled as possibilities rather than proven root causes.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make visible the specific dispatch-clarification problem connected to at least three labeled category branches, with proposed causes placed beneath their corresponding categories. Keep the organization of possible causes distinct from subsequent analysis and agreement on actions.

teaching_notes: Do not add mandatory cause-category lists or infer cause from number of suggestions.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

coverage.learning_objective: Learner can define and apply a Definition of Done (DoD) as the team-wide quality bar every backlog item must meet before being called complete.

required_facts.statement: The Definition of Done describes the state of an increment when it meets the required quality measures.
The Scrum Team follows a shared Definition of Done, at least as rigorous as any organizational standard.
An item that does not meet the Definition of Done cannot be released or presented at the Sprint Review.
Check the completed work against the defined quality criteria and identify any unmet criterion before calling it done.
Story acceptance criteria specify completion conditions for that particular story rather than replacing the shared quality standard.

teaching_blocks.content: Imagine a team has a shared Definition of Done for an increment. In this hypothetical standard, required quality measures include passing the agreed checks and completing the agreed review. The exact checks are invented for the exercise; the shared standard must be at least as rigorous as any applicable organizational standard.

teaching_blocks.title: Definition of Done
teaching_blocks.content: The Definition of Done describes the state of an increment when it meets the required quality measures.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: The Scrum Team follows a shared Definition of Done, at least as rigorous as any organizational standard. An item that does not meet the Definition of Done cannot be released or presented at the Sprint Review. Check the completed work against the defined quality criteria and identify any unmet criterion before calling it done. Story acceptance criteria specify completion conditions for that particular story rather than replacing the shared quality standard.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Before calling work done, check it against every defined quality criterion and identify unmet criteria. If one required review remains incomplete, the item does not meet the Definition of Done. Under the stated Scrum rule, an item that does not meet it cannot be released or presented at the Sprint Review.

Now compare that with a story’s acceptance condition, such as “Selecting an existing order displays current instructions.” The condition specifies completion for this particular story. Even if the behavior satisfies that condition, it does not replace the shared quality standard. The learner needs to distinguish story-specific behavior from the state required of the increment.

The useful output is a clear check against the shared standard, not a subjective declaration that the work looks finished. Keep unmet criteria visible and do not quietly lower the standard to match what was completed. The BA can help clarify story conditions while the Scrum Team follows the shared Definition of Done.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Passing a story’s acceptance criteria does not replace the shared Definition of Done. An item with an unmet required quality criterion cannot be labeled done, released, or presented at Sprint Review under the Definition of Done rule. Do not reinterpret that as merely optional reporting guidance.

video_need.reason: The distinction and the worked business example can be understood from prose; one simple annotated visual is sufficient and a motion demonstration would mostly repeat the text.

practice_anchor.objective: Check a completed order-instructions item against a supplied five-point Definition of Done checklist. Use the supplied evidence for each criterion and select every unmet criterion. Treat the checklist as a hypothetical shared standard that meets applicable organizational requirements.
practice_anchor.success: Every unmet criterion is selected and no satisfied criterion is flagged. A completed story acceptance condition is not treated as a substitute for the shared standard, and any unmet required criterion prevents the item from being marked done, released, or presented at Sprint Review.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the hypothetical five-point shared Definition of Done visible alongside evidence and met/unmet status for the completed order-instructions item. Show the story-specific acceptance condition separately and highlight how an incomplete required review prevents done status, release, and presentation at Sprint Review.

teaching_notes: Preserve the release/review restriction and organizational-standard floor explicitly.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

context.concept_name: Star Schema / Dimensional Modeling for BI

coverage.learning_objective: Learner can design a star schema (fact and dimension tables) for a BI data model to support efficient analytical queries.

required_facts.statement: A star schema separates tables describing business entities from tables storing observations or events.
Dimension tables describe entities and their attributes; their key columns identify rows.
Fact tables store observations or events with dimension keys and often numeric measures.
Choose the fact table’s grain so its rows describe a consistent level of detail.
Connect dimension tables to the central fact table through one-to-many relationships using the dimension’s unique key.
source_refs: powerbi_docs#https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/power-bi/guidance/star-schema — Star schema relevance to Power BI semantic models

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose a BI model needs to report order amounts by customer and branch. A star schema separates the observations or events from tables that describe business entities.

teaching_blocks.title: Star Schema / Dimensional Modeling for BI
teaching_blocks.content: A star schema separates tables describing business entities from tables storing observations or events.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Dimension tables describe entities and their attributes; their key columns identify rows. Fact tables store observations or events with dimension keys and often numeric measures. Choose the fact table’s grain so its rows describe a consistent level of detail. Connect dimension tables to the central fact table through one-to-many relationships using the dimension’s unique key.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
For this hypothetical model, choose the fact grain as one row per order. OrderFact stores order observations, dimension keys, and a numeric amount. CustomerDim and BranchDim describe their entities and attributes, with unique key columns identifying their rows. Connect those dimensions to the central fact table using one-to-many relationships through each dimension’s unique key.

The grain decision keeps the fact rows at a consistent level of detail. Do not mix one row per order with one row per branch-month total in that same example fact table and then describe all rows as equivalent observations. The dimension tables provide descriptive information, while the fact table holds the chosen observations or events and often numeric measures.

The useful mental model is a central fact table surrounded by descriptive dimensions. Keys connect an observation to the relevant descriptions. The example uses numeric Amount; fact tables often have numeric measures, but their fields reflect the observations or events being modeled.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A fact table and a dimension table are not interchangeable because both contain columns. Dimensions describe entities; facts store observations or events at a consistent grain. Mixing detail levels in the example would defeat that grain decision.

video_need.reason: Arranging dimensions around a fact table and highlighting a consistent row grain makes the star structure clear.

media.group_title: Separate business events from descriptive dimensions

segments.label: A central sales table surrounded by descriptive tables
segments.summary: In a hypothetical chocolate business, a sales table records sales details but cannot alone explain a salesperson’s team, a product’s characteristics, or a geography’s region. Separate salesperson, product, and geography tables supply those descriptions. Connections between the sales table and these surrounding tables form the star structure: business observations sit at the center, with descriptive business-entity tables around them.

segments.label: Fact-table events and dimension-table descriptions
segments.summary: A fact table records business events or activity. The sales example includes IDs linking to other tables, event dates, and numeric measures such as quantity and sales. Fact tables often contain numeric measures used in calculations. Dimension tables describe business entities: the product example includes attributes such as name, category, brand, and color. These descriptions provide context for filtering and grouping results. In sales by category, the sales numbers come from facts, while category comes from a dimension.

bridge_note.before: Watch the first clip’s central sales table and surrounding descriptions, then the second clip’s fact–dimension contrast. The first creator’s “central” and “outer concepts” correspond here to the fact table and dimensions.
bridge_note.after: The first clip illustrates the star structure; the second explains events, linked IDs, measures, and descriptive attributes. Neither establishes unique dimension keys, consistent fact grain, or one-to-many relationships; the text teaches those requirements.

practice_anchor.objective: Design a star schema for a hypothetical order-reporting process using one fact table and three dimensions: customer, branch, and order date. Declare one row per order, assign supplied descriptive fields and keys to the dimensions, and assign dimension keys and Amount to OrderFact.
practice_anchor.success: The design contains one central OrderFact and exactly three descriptive dimensions. Every fact row represents one order. Each dimension has a unique row-identifying key, OrderFact contains the corresponding dimension keys and Amount, and each dimension connects to OrderFact through a one-to-many relationship.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make a central OrderFact surrounded by customer, branch, and order-date dimensions visible. Show descriptive attributes, unique dimension keys, corresponding fact-table keys, one-to-many connections, and an explicit one-row-per-order grain annotation.

teaching_notes: Preserve “often” for numeric measures; do not add unsupported dimensional modeling types.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

context.concept_name: Data Model Relationships in BI Tools

coverage.learning_objective: Learner can define relationships between tables within a BI tool's data model so visuals can query across them correctly.

required_facts.statement: Model relationships propagate filters between related tables so a visual can use fields from multiple tables.
Use Modeling > Manage relationships > New and choose the two tables and their matching columns.
Set cardinality according to the uniqueness of values on each side and check the active relationship setting.
Choose cross-filter direction deliberately: Single propagates filters in one direction and Both allows propagation in both directions.

teaching_blocks.content: Imagine a Power BI model with CustomerDim and OrderFact. A visual uses customer descriptions and order amounts, so the model relationship needs to propagate filters between related tables.

teaching_blocks.title: Data Model Relationships in BI Tools
teaching_blocks.content: Model relationships propagate filters between related tables so a visual can use fields from multiple tables.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Use Modeling > Manage relationships > New and choose the two tables and their matching columns. Set cardinality according to the uniqueness of values on each side and check the active relationship setting. Choose cross-filter direction deliberately: Single propagates filters in one direction and Both allows propagation in both directions.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Use Modeling > Manage relationships > New and choose the two tables and matching columns. For this hypothetical data, CustomerDim.CustomerID is unique and OrderFact.CustomerID repeats across orders, so set cardinality according to that uniqueness and check the active relationship setting.

Choose cross-filter direction deliberately. Single propagates filters in one direction; Both allows propagation in both directions. These are different choices, not an instruction to select Both whenever a report has more than one table. The direction must be considered for the intended filter behavior.

The useful output is a relationship whose matching columns, cardinality, active setting, and filtering direction are understood. If a report combines fields from both tables, explain how the relationship enables filters to reach related data rather than assuming that similar column names are enough. The example stops at the supported relationship settings and does not invent automatic conflict resolution or a universal recommendation for every model.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A relationship is not just a line for display: it propagates filters. Also, Both is not automatically the best setting; it permits two-way propagation and should be chosen deliberately. Check uniqueness and the active setting rather than assuming them.

video_need.reason: Creating a relationship and examining cardinality, active state, and filter direction benefits from tool demonstration.

media.group_title: How relationship direction controls filter propagation

segments.label: Single and Both cross-filter directions between related tables
segments.summary: Relationship filter direction determines whether a filter can travel from one table to another. In the sales-and-segments example, Single direction from sales to segments lets a customer filter on sales affect the segments total, but filtering segments does not affect sales. Reversing Single direction reverses which table can filter the other. Both permits filters to propagate in either direction between these two tables. These settings control how related data responds to filtering; neither direction is presented here as a universal requirement.

bridge_note.before: Watch how filtering sales or segments affects the other table under Single and Both. Treat the clip’s “everything filters everything” wording as referring to this two-table example, not every table in any model.
bridge_note.after: The clip demonstrates filter propagation and direction, but not relationship creation, cardinality configuration, or the active setting. The text covers those steps using CustomerDim and OrderFact.

practice_anchor.objective: Configure a relationship between imported CustomerDim and OrderFact tables through Modeling > Manage relationships > New. Match CustomerID in both tables, use the supplied uniqueness information to set cardinality, check the active setting, and choose Single so CustomerDim filters OrderFact.
practice_anchor.success: The saved relationship connects CustomerDim.CustomerID to OrderFact.CustomerID, with CustomerDim on the one side and OrderFact on the many side. The relationship is active, and Single direction permits CustomerDim to filter OrderFact. The learner can explain why a CustomerDim filter reaches related orders and why the reverse propagation is not enabled.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show the relationship settings and resulting model connection between CustomerDim.CustomerID and OrderFact.CustomerID, making the one-to-many cardinality, active setting, and Single filter direction from CustomerDim to OrderFact visible.

teaching_notes: No unsupported defaults or claims that bidirectional filtering is universally preferred.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content:

Use color consistently and avoid unnecessary variation or decoration that distracts from the data. Reduce unnecessary views and labels so the intended comparison stays readable. context.concept_name: Power BI Measures and Calculated Columns (DAX)

coverage.learning_objective: Learner can write DAX measures and calculated columns in Power BI to compute business metrics.

required_facts.statement: A DAX measure calculates a result that changes with the current report filtering and selection context.
Use Modeling > New measure and enter MeasureName = SUM(TableName[NumericColumn]) to define a basic total that responds to report context.
A calculated column uses a DAX expression to calculate a value for each row rather than the measure’s report-context result.
Use New Column and write column_name = expression; the formula is applied across the table’s rows.
In standard Import mode, calculated-column values are materialized and refreshed when the underlying data is refreshed.

For a classic date-column time-intelligence calculation, use a marked date table whose Date or date/time column contains unique, nonblank dates without gaps and spans full years, including the periods being compared.
Relate the date table to the metric table’s relevant date column with an active relationship so that report filters on the date table propagate to the metric’s rows.
source_refs: powerbi_docs#https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/power-bi/guidance/relationships-active-inactive — Active relationships; Inactive relationships — active OrderDate relationship and filter propagation

required_facts.statement: Evaluate the base total measure in the current date filter context and obtain its corresponding prior-year value with PriorYear = CALCULATE([MeasureName], SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR('Date'[Date])), which evaluates that measure with the dates shifted one year back.

Compute year-over-year growth with Growth = DIVIDE([MeasureName] - [PriorYear], [PriorYear]) and format it as a percentage; without an alternate result, DIVIDE returns BLANK when the prior-year denominator is zero or blank.
source_refs: powerbi_docs#https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dax/best-practices/dax-divide-function-operator — DIVIDE syntax and zero or BLANK denominator behavior

teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose OrderFact contains Amount and Quantity. A measure can total Amount while responding to current report filters. Use Modeling > New measure and enter:
TotalAmount = SUM(OrderFact[Amount])
With hypothetical North amounts 40 and 60 and South amount 30, the unfiltered total is 130 and the North-filtered total is 100.

teaching_blocks.title: Power BI Measures and Calculated Columns (DAX)
teaching_blocks.content: A DAX measure calculates a result that changes with the current report filtering and selection context.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Use Modeling > New measure and enter MeasureName = SUM(TableName[NumericColumn]) to define a basic total that responds to report context. A calculated column uses a DAX expression to calculate a value for each row rather than the measure’s report-context result. Use New Column and write column_name = expression; the formula is applied across the table’s rows. In standard Import mode, calculated-column values are materialized and refreshed when the underlying data is refreshed. For a classic date-column time-intelligence calculation, use a marked date table whose Date or date/time column contains unique, nonblank dates without gaps and spans full years, including the periods being compared. Relate the date table to the metric table’s relevant date column with an active relationship so that report filters on the date table propagate to the metric’s rows. Evaluate the base total measure in the current date filter context and obtain its corresponding prior-year value with PriorYear = CALCULATE([MeasureName], SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR('Date'[Date])), which evaluates that measure with the dates shifted one year back. Compute year-over-year growth with Growth = DIVIDE([MeasureName] - [PriorYear], [PriorYear]) and format it as a percentage; without an alternate result, DIVIDE returns BLANK when the prior-year denominator is zero or blank.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
A calculated column instead evaluates an expression for each row. Use New Column and enter:
DoubleQuantity = OrderFact[Quantity] * 2
Rows with quantities 2 and 3 receive 4 and 6. In standard Import mode these values are materialized and refreshed when underlying data is refreshed; do not describe them as the same report-context calculation as a measure.

For the classic date-column prior-year pattern, first use a marked date table with unique, nonblank, gap-free dates spanning full years and the compared periods. Relate it actively to the fact table’s relevant date column so date filters propagate. Then define:
PriorYear = CALCULATE([TotalAmount], SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR('Date'[Date]))
This evaluates the base measure with dates shifted one year back. Define growth with:
Growth = DIVIDE([TotalAmount] - [PriorYear], [PriorYear])
and format it as a percentage.

For an example current total of 120 and corresponding prior-year total of 100, growth is (120 − 100) / 100 = 20%. Without an alternate result, DIVIDE returns BLANK when the denominator is zero or blank. Keep the date prerequisites visible: the formula is not a substitute for the marked date table and active relationship required by this pattern.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Measures and calculated columns are not two names for the same evaluation. The measure responds to report context; the column calculates each row and, in standard Import mode, materializes values on refresh. For growth, divide the difference by prior year—not current year—and do not omit the date-table prerequisites.

video_need.reason: Creating measures and columns, changing filters, and checking date-model prerequisites makes evaluation context and time comparison visible.

These conditions supplement the initial visual filter context. The same principle applies to Power BI visuals: CALCULATE can change the filter context in which a measure is evaluated.

coverage.learning_objective: Learner can write Tableau calculated fields to compute derived business metrics within a workbook.

required_facts.statement: A Tableau calculated field derives new data from existing fields without changing the original source.
Choose Analysis > Create Calculated Field, name the field, enter an expression, and select OK.
The source’s Discount Ratio calculation is IIF([Sales] !=0, [Discount]/[Sales],0): it returns Discount divided by Sales when Sales is nonzero, and zero otherwise.
source_refs: tableau_help#https://help.tableau.com/current/pro/desktop/en-us/calculations_calculatedfields_create.htm — Create a calculated field — Discount Ratio example

required_facts.statement: A basic calculation may operate at the row level or at the visualization’s aggregate level, depending on its expression.
Numeric calculated fields can be summed automatically when added to a view; change the aggregation if the intended metric requires a different one.
source_refs: tableau_help#https://help.tableau.com/current/pro/desktop/en-us/calculations_calculatedfields_create.htm — Use a calculated field in the view

teaching_blocks.content:
Imagine a Tableau source with Sales and Discount. A calculated field derives new data from existing fields without changing the original source. Use Analysis > Create Calculated Field, name the field Discount Ratio, enter the expression, and select OK:
IIF([Sales] !=0, [Discount]/[Sales],0)

teaching_blocks.title: Tableau Calculated Fields
teaching_blocks.content: A Tableau calculated field derives new data from existing fields without changing the original source.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Choose Analysis > Create Calculated Field, name the field, enter an expression, and select OK. The Discount Ratio calculation is IIF([Sales] !=0, [Discount]/[Sales],0): it returns Discount divided by Sales when Sales is nonzero, and zero otherwise. A basic calculation may operate at the row level or at the visualization’s aggregate level, depending on its expression. Numeric calculated fields can be summed automatically when added to a view; change the aggregation if the intended metric requires a different one.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
For hypothetical rows with Sales 100 and Discount 10, and Sales 0 and Discount 0, the calculated values are 0.1 and 0. The expression returns Discount divided by Sales when Sales is nonzero, and zero otherwise. It does not establish that a missing value behaves like zero; this example uses known numeric values only.

A basic calculation can operate at row level or at the visualization’s aggregate level, depending on the expression. Numeric calculated fields can be summed automatically when added to a view, so inspect whether that aggregation fits the intended metric. With rows having ratios 0.1 and 0.2, summing the row ratios gives 0.3; do not label that automatically as the intended business discount metric.

The useful output is a calculated field with an understood expression and a deliberate view aggregation. Creating the field and deciding how to summarize it are separate analytical concerns.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A calculated field does not modify the original source. Also, a numeric field’s automatic sum is not proof that sum is the appropriate metric. Inspect the expression’s level and choose aggregation for the business question rather than blindly accepting the initial view.

video_need.reason: Creating the field and checking how its numeric values aggregate in a view benefits from a tool demonstration.

This directly entered calculation is available only in that view.

Reports can reuse an existing published semantic model rather than each creating separate data and calculation definitions.
source_refs: powerbi_docs#https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/power-bi/connect-data/service-datasets-across-workspaces — Discover semantic models; Copy a report

source_refs: powerbi_docs#https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/power-bi/connect-data/service-datasets-across-workspaces — Discover semantic models; Build permission for semantic models

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose operations and sales each need a report using the same total-order-amount calculation. A Power BI semantic model contains data-model logic that reports can use. Reusing one published model avoids having each report create separate data and calculation definitions for this shared need.

teaching_blocks.title: BI Semantic Layer
teaching_blocks.content: A Power BI semantic model contains data-model logic that can be used to build reports.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Reports can reuse an existing published semantic model rather than each creating separate data and calculation definitions. Define the shared business calculation as a measure in the common model and use that model for reports that need the same calculation. Connect a new report to the existing shared semantic model; building content on a shared model requires Build permission.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
For this hypothetical arrangement, define the shared business calculation as a measure in the common model. Build both reports from that model when they need the same calculation. One report may focus on branches and another on customers while using the shared calculation definition.

Connect a new report to the existing shared semantic model. Building content on it requires Build permission, so do not assume access to a finished report automatically grants authority to build new content from its model.

The useful mental model is shared data-model logic supporting multiple reports, rather than every report independently recreating the same business calculation. The example does not promise every report will display the same result under different filters; it is the common calculation definition that is reused. Keep the distinction between shared model, report, and required Build permission clear.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Sharing a calculation definition does not mean every differently filtered report displays an identical number. Reports reuse model logic. Also, building new content on the shared model requires Build permission; do not treat mere report access as that permission.

video_need.reason: A model-to-multiple-reports diagram can clarify shared calculations and the separate Build permission requirement.

media.group_title: One shared semantic model, multiple reports

segments.label: Reuse a published Power BI semantic model across reports
segments.summary: A semantic model holds the data and model logic, including tables, source connections, transformations, relationships, measures, and field formatting. The presenter calls this object a dataset and distinguishes it from a report. After explaining publication to the Power BI service, he creates a report connected to an existing model rather than a separate model of its own. He adds a sales visualization, saves the report, and uses the lineage view to show that one model supplies four reports.

segments.label: Build permission for reports using a shared semantic model
segments.summary: Shared semantic models let report creators reuse a model in a workspace, including for reports stored in another workspace. The presenter uses the term shared datasets. Creating a report from a shared model requires Build permission for the relevant user or group. Reusing existing models across reports helps reduce isolated, separately maintained data definitions.

bridge_note.before: Both clips use “dataset” for a Power BI semantic model. Watch the first for model reuse and lineage, and the second for the separate Build permission requirement.
bridge_note.after: The first clip demonstrates reuse but omits Build permission; the second explains that requirement. Neither demonstrates defining the shared business measure. The text covers that centralization step as well as reuse and permission.

practice_anchor.objective: In a simplified model-and-report configuration, consolidate the total-order-amount calculation duplicated in the operations and sales reports into one measure in a common published semantic model. Connect both reports to that model and specify the required Build permission.
practice_anchor.success: One shared total-order-amount measure is defined in the common model, and both reports use that model instead of maintaining separate calculation definitions. Build permission is identified as required for creating report content from the shared model; differently filtered reports need not display identical totals.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show the operations and sales reports initially maintaining separate total-order-amount definitions, then both connected to one published semantic model containing the shared measure. Mark Build permission as a requirement for creating report content, and distinguish a shared definition from potentially different filtered results.

teaching_notes: Do not invent connection UI steps; distinguish shared definition from filtered result.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

clusters.title: Gathering requirements evidence
clusters.reasoning: These adjacent concepts are complementary channels for gathering requirements evidence: survey responses, existing documents, and observed work. Problem scoping, their shared prerequisite, is complete before this tile starts. Keep each channel separately labeled so stated attitudes, recorded material, and observed behavior are not treated as interchangeable evidence. Validation remains a separate step because its document-analysis prerequisite is not available at tile start.

clusters.title: Describing business data and identifying rows
clusters.reasoning: These adjacent concepts belong to the same initial data-description task: identify business entities and their descriptive attributes, then consider which column or columns uniquely identify table rows. Neither concept has a prerequisite in the inputs. Separate sub-concepts preserve the distinction between a descriptive attribute and a primary key with uniqueness and non-null requirements. Foreign keys stay outside this cluster because primary keys are their prerequisite within this tile.

clusters.title: Connecting BI tools to business data
clusters.reasoning: These adjacent concepts are tool-specific variants of connecting to and preparing a data source for BI work. Their relational-model prerequisite is already complete at tile start. Retain separate Power BI and Tableau sub-concepts and their own preparation commands; grouping does not imply that Power Query transformations and Tableau joins or extracts are the same operation.

clusters.title: Establishing the current and desired states
clusters.reasoning: These adjacent concepts establish the paired baseline and target for a state comparison. Their respective as-is and to-be modeling prerequisites are both complete before the tile starts. Separate current-state and desired-state labels preserve the essential distinction between the present situation and intended outcomes. Gap identification and SWOT remain separate because they depend on concepts introduced within this tile.

clusters.title: Requirements-prioritization methods
clusters.reasoning: These adjacent concepts are variants of requirements prioritization. Their shared business-requirements-document prerequisite is complete before the tile starts. Preserve separate labels for MoSCoW priority categories, Kano satisfaction categories, and weighted-scoring ranking so grouping does not hide the distinctions between the methods.

clusters.title: Writing findings for the audience
clusters.reasoning: These adjacent concepts are complementary parts of one communication task: structure a written report and adapt its detail and terminology to the audience. Neither has a prerequisite in the inputs. Keep report structure and audience adaptation as distinct sub-concepts rather than replacing either with a general communication lesson. Presentations and walkthroughs stay separate because their prerequisites are introduced within this tile.

clusters.title: Defining business metrics in BI tools
clusters.reasoning: These adjacent concepts are tool-specific variants of deriving business metrics from existing data. Both dashboard-design prerequisites and reporting-query patterns are complete before this tile starts. Preserve distinct Power BI DAX and Tableau calculation sub-concepts, including their own row-level and aggregate or report-context distinctions; no equivalence between their evaluation rules is implied. The semantic layer remains a later step because it requires both calculation concepts.
